title: EPIC in New York: lower drug costs for people 65 and older
seoTitle: EPIC NY: Income Limits, Copays and How to Apply
seoDesc: EPIC helps New Yorkers 65+ pay for prescriptions. See income limits, the Fee and Deductible Plans, $3 to $20 copays, how it works with Part D, and how to apply.
dek: EPIC is New York's drug coverage program for people 65 and older. It works with Medicare Part D to bring most prescriptions down to $3 to $20. Here is who qualifies and how to apply.
keyFacts: Age 65 or older and a New York resident
Income up to $75,000 single or $100,000 married
Must have, or be able to get, Medicare Part D
Copays of $3 to $20 after Part D pays
EPIC Helpline: 1-800-332-3742
body:
The Elderly Pharmaceutical Insurance Coverage (EPIC) program is New York State's prescription program for people 65 and older, and it works alongside Medicare Part D to cut what you pay at the pharmacy. If your mom or dad lives in New York, has income up to $75,000 (single) or $100,000 (married), and has or can get a Part D plan, they can join at any time of year.

EPIC is run by the New York State Department of Health. It sits behind your Part D plan as secondary coverage. Part D pays first, then EPIC lowers what is left to a copay of $3 to $20. For people with lower incomes, EPIC can also pay part or all of the monthly Part D premium. This guide covers who qualifies, the two EPIC plans, the copays, how EPIC fits with Extra Help, and how to apply.

Who qualifies for EPIC?

The state lists four rules. You must:

  • Live in New York State and be 65 or older. New York has to be your permanent home, where you live on a regular basis. A summer or winter home here does not count.
  • Have yearly income below the limit. That means up to $75,000 if single or $100,000 if married.
  • Be enrolled in Part D, or be eligible to enroll. The state says there are no exceptions. A Medicare Advantage HMO plan counts only if it includes Part D drug coverage.
  • Not be getting full Medicaid benefits.

You also cannot join if you have neither Medicare Part A nor Part B, or if your union or retiree drug coverage is not a Part D plan.

What counts as income?

EPIC looks at the previous calendar year's total income for you, or for you and your spouse. It includes Social Security (minus Medicare premiums), pensions and taxable IRA distributions. It leaves out things like SNAP (food stamps), Medicare premiums and Medicaid. For people who file federal taxes, EPIC starts from adjusted gross income, minus Medicare Part B premiums. So a widow in Rochester whose Social Security and pension came to $28,000 last year would be measured against the single limit.

Part D pays first. EPIC then brings your share down to $3 to $20 a prescription.

What is the difference between the Fee Plan and the Deductible Plan?

EPIC puts every member into one of two plans based on income. You do not choose. EPIC places you based on last year's income.

EPIC planSingle incomeMarried incomeWhat you pay EPIC
Fee PlanUp to $20,000Up to $26,000An annual fee of $8 to $300, based on last year's income
Deductible Plan$20,001 to $75,000$26,001 to $100,000An annual deductible, based on income, before EPIC copays start
Part D premium helpUp to $23,000Up to $29,000EPIC pays Part D premiums up to a set basic amount

The Fee Plan

Fee Plan members pay EPIC a yearly fee. You can pay it once a year or in a bill every three months. The fee rises with income. On the state's fee schedule, a single person with income up to $6,000 pays $8 a year, and a single person with $19,001 to $20,000 pays $230. Married members pay a fee for each person, from $8 each at the bottom up to $300 each for joint income of $25,001 to $26,000. EPIC also pays the Part D premium, up to a basic amount, for Fee Plan members.

The Deductible Plan

Deductible Plan members pay no fee. Instead, they must meet a yearly EPIC deductible, based on last year's income, before EPIC copays begin. Once you meet it, you pay EPIC copays for the rest of the year. The coverage year ends December 31.

If your income is $20,001 to $23,000 (single) or $26,001 to $29,000 (married), EPIC also pays your Part D premium up to the basic amount. Above that, you pay your own Part D premium each month. To make up for that, EPIC lowers your deductible by about the yearly cost of a basic Part D plan. The exact deductible for each income band is on the schedule linked from the EPIC Deductible Plan page.

How much are EPIC copays?

EPIC copays depend on what is left of the drug's price after Part D has paid. They apply once any Part D deductible is met, and once Deductible Plan members have met the EPIC deductible.

Cost left after Part DYour EPIC copay
Up to $15$3
$15.01 to $35$7
$35.01 to $55$15
Over $55$20

Say your dad in Syracuse fills a brand-name prescription and his Part D plan leaves him owing $100. With EPIC, he pays $20 instead. EPIC covers approved Part D drugs. Once you have Part D, it can also cover approved drugs that Part D leaves out.

Part D itself now caps what you spend in a year. Medicare says that once your out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027), you pay nothing more for covered drugs that year. EPIC helps with the costs you face before that point.

How does EPIC work with Part D and Extra Help?

EPIC never replaces Part D. If you are not in a Part D plan, EPIC gives you no drug coverage at all. EPIC is secondary coverage, so its benefits are built to sit on top of a Part D plan.

Joining EPIC gives you a Special Enrollment Period, so a new member can sign up for a Part D plan at any time of the year. After that, members can change Medicare drug plans once per calendar year using EPIC. That is on top of the regular fall open enrollment from October 15 to December 7 (see our Medicare open enrollment guide).

Extra Help comes first

Extra Help (also called the Low Income Subsidy) is the federal program that lowers Part D premiums, deductibles and copays. EPIC requires income-eligible members to apply for it. You can do that right on the EPIC application, and EPIC will apply on your behalf. EPIC also sends your application to New York Medicaid to see if you qualify for a Medicare Savings Program.

The payoff can be large. Members who are approved for Extra Help, a Medicare Savings Program or Medicaid spenddown pay no EPIC fees. Read more in our guides to Extra Help and the Medicare Savings Program.

Using EPIC and Extra Help together

Extra Help lowers your Part D costs first. EPIC then works on what is left. The state says members with Extra Help pay no EPIC fee and get lower EPIC copayments.

How do I apply for EPIC?

There is one application, and no deadline. You do not have to send proof of income. EPIC checks your information with the Social Security Administration and the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance.

  1. Get the application. Apply online at nyepic.primetherapeutics.com, or call the EPIC Helpline at 1-800-332-3742 (TTY 1-800-290-9138) and ask for a paper form. The line is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.
  2. Fill in income for last year. Have last year's Social Security statement (SSA-1099), pension statements and tax return handy so the numbers match what the state sees.
  3. Check the Extra Help box. If your income is low enough, let EPIC apply for Extra Help for you. It costs nothing and can wipe out your EPIC fee.
  4. Send it in. Mail it to EPIC, P.O. Box 15018, Albany, NY 12212-5018. The state also takes faxed applications. Call the helpline for the fax number.
  5. Pick or keep a Part D plan. If you are not in a plan yet, use your Special Enrollment Period to join one. Benefits do not start until you are enrolled in Part D.
  6. Watch the mail. Fee Plan members are billed every three months or can pay once a year. EPIC also writes when it is time to renew.

Fee payments go by mail to State of NY Health Department, PO Box 789865, Philadelphia, PA 19178-9865. Write your EPIC ID number on the check.

Is it different in New York City?

No. EPIC is a statewide program with one helpline and one mailing address, so the rules are the same in Queens, Buffalo or Plattsburgh. What differs is where you get free help filling things out. The Health Insurance Information, Counseling and Assistance Program (HIICAP) has counselors in local offices for the aging across the state. Call the state HIICAP line at 1-800-701-0501, say your county or borough, and you will be routed to your local HIICAP program. They can compare Part D plans with EPIC in mind. NY Connects can point you to other local help.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Dropping Part D. EPIC ends when Part D ends. Never cancel a Part D plan because you think EPIC will cover you.
  • Skipping Extra Help. People who qualify for both and never apply for Extra Help can end up paying EPIC fees they could have avoided.
  • Waiting for open enrollment. You can join EPIC any month, and joining opens a window to pick a Part D plan.
  • Forgetting address changes. EPIC requires you to report a move. If your mom moves from Yonkers to live with you in Albany, call the helpline.
  • Ignoring the renewal notice. EPIC tells you by mail when you must renew. Answer it and keep it with your Medicare papers.

If your parent has very high drug costs and income over the Medicaid limit, EPIC also helps with Medicaid spenddown. The full cost EPIC pays for prescriptions counts toward a Medicaid excess income amount, which our Medicaid guide explains.

faq.q: How do I get my mom help paying for prescriptions in Queens?
faq.a: If she is 65 or older, has a Part D plan and income up to $75,000 (or $100,000 with a spouse), she can join EPIC. Apply online at nyepic.primetherapeutics.com or call 1-800-332-3742. Ask EPIC to apply for Extra Help at the same time.

faq.q: My dad in Buffalo has a Medicare Advantage plan. Can he still use EPIC?
faq.a: Yes, if his Medicare Advantage plan includes Part D drug coverage. EPIC requires Part D, either a stand-alone plan or a Medicare Advantage HMO plan that includes it.

faq.q: Can I get EPIC if I have Medicaid?
faq.a: Not if you get full Medicaid benefits. People on Medicaid spenddown can be EPIC members, and they pay no EPIC fees.

faq.q: Do I have to send tax returns with the EPIC application?
faq.a: No. EPIC checks your income with the Social Security Administration and the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance. Use last year's income when you fill out the form.

faq.q: When can I join EPIC?
faq.a: Any time of year. Joining also gives you a Special Enrollment Period to sign up for a Part D plan if you do not have one.

faq.q: What is the EPIC phone number?
faq.a: The EPIC Helpline is 1-800-332-3742 (TTY 1-800-290-9138), open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

title: Extra Help for Medicare drug costs in New York: 2027 guide
seoTitle: Extra Help Medicare NY: 2027 Copays and Limits
seoDesc: Extra Help cuts Medicare drug costs to $5.80 generic and $14.40 brand in 2027. See the limits, how New Yorkers get it automatically, and how it works with EPIC.
dek: Extra Help cuts Part D costs to a few dollars a prescription. Many New Yorkers get it automatically through the Medicare Savings Program, even with savings. Here is how.
keyFacts: 2027 copays: up to $5.80 generic, $14.40 brand
$0 Part D deductible with Extra Help in 2027
2026 limits: income $23,940 single, resources $18,090
Automatic with Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program or SSI
Social Security: 1-800-772-1213
body:
Extra Help is the federal program that lowers Medicare Part D drug costs for people with limited income and savings. In 2027, Medicare says people with Extra Help pay no Part D deductible and no more than $5.80 for a generic drug or $14.40 for a brand-name drug.

Extra Help is also called the Low Income Subsidy, or LIS. Social Security runs the application, but many New Yorkers who get it never fill out a Social Security form at all. They get it automatically through New York's Medicare Savings Program or Medicaid. This guide explains the 2026 limits, the 2027 copays, the automatic routes that work so well in New York, and how Extra Help fits with EPIC.

What does Extra Help pay in 2027?

Extra Help helps with your Part D plan premium and deductible and caps your copays. Medicare lists these amounts for 2027:

CostWith Extra Help in 2027
Part D deductible$0
Generic drugsUp to $5.80 each at a participating pharmacy
Brand-name drugsUp to $14.40 each at a participating pharmacy
People with full Medicaid who are also in QMBNo more than $4.90 for each covered drug
After drug costs reach $2,400$0 for each covered drug
Part D late enrollment penaltyNone while you get Extra Help

To see what that saves, compare it with a standard plan. Medicare says no Part D plan may have a deductible above $700 in 2027, and out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs is capped at $2,400 in 2027. With Extra Help, you skip the deductible entirely and pay small fixed copays on the way to that cap.

One note on premiums. If your parent picks a plan with a higher premium, Extra Help may not cover all of it. The New York State Department of Health notes that EPIC can then help Extra Help members in enhanced or Medicare Advantage plans with premiums, up to the basic amount, after Medicare's subsidy.

There is one more benefit families often miss. Medicare says you will not owe a Part D late enrollment penalty while you get Extra Help. So if your mom skipped Part D when she turned 65 and has been worried about a penalty, Extra Help takes that worry off the table for as long as she has it. That makes it a good moment to join a plan.

What it looks like at the pharmacy

Say your dad in Binghamton takes three generic drugs and one brand-name drug each month. With Extra Help in 2027, the most he would pay is $5.80 for each generic and $14.40 for the brand. That comes to $31.80 a month at most, or $381.60 over a full year, with no deductible first. Without Extra Help, he could face a deductible of up to $700 before his plan's regular copays begin.

In New York, the Medicare Savings Program has no savings test, and it brings Extra Help with it.

Who qualifies for Extra Help?

You need Medicare and income and resources under federal limits. Medicare lists the 2026 limits below. The 2027 limits had not been posted on Medicare.gov as of November 25, 2026.

2026 limitsYearly incomeResources
Single$23,940$18,090
Married couple$32,460$36,100

If your income or savings are close to the line, apply anyway. Social Security looks at the details, and Medicare says you can reapply any time if your income or resources change.

How do New Yorkers get Extra Help automatically?

Medicare says you qualify for Extra Help automatically if you get any of these:

  • Full Medicaid coverage.
  • A Medicare Savings Program, where the state pays your Part B premium.
  • Supplemental Security Income (SSI) from Social Security.

The Medicare Savings Program route is the big one in New York. The state's Medicare Savings Program has no resource test, so savings do not count. The 2026 income limit for the QI level is $2,474 a month for a single person and $3,355 for a couple. NYC's Human Resources Administration (HRA) states that Medicare consumers who qualify for MSP automatically qualify for the Low Income Subsidy.

Put that together and you get a useful result. Say your mom lives in Albany, gets $2,200 a month from Social Security, and has $45,000 in savings. Her savings are well above the Extra Help resource limit, so a direct Extra Help application would not meet the resource test. But she can qualify for the Medicare Savings Program, because New York does not count savings for it, and that brings Extra Help with it. Read our Medicare Savings Program guide for the application steps.

Apply for both at once

Medicare says you can apply for Extra Help and the Medicare Savings Program at the same time. In New York, applying for the MSP is often the stronger move if your parent has savings.

How do I apply for Extra Help directly?

If your parent does not qualify for the Medicare Savings Program or Medicaid, apply through Social Security. Social Security says you can apply any time, before or after joining a Part D plan.

  1. Gather the numbers. Have recent bank and investment statements, Social Security and pension amounts, and the Medicare card ready.
  2. Apply online or by phone. Apply at ssa.gov/medicare/part-d-extra-help. Or call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m., and ask for an appointment to apply for Part D Extra Help.
  3. Or let EPIC apply for you. If your parent is 65 or older and applying for EPIC, check the Extra Help box on the EPIC application. EPIC will apply on their behalf.
  4. Make sure they have a Part D plan. Extra Help pays toward a Part D plan, so your parent needs one.
  5. Check the next pharmacy receipt. Once approved, copays should drop. If they do not, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

What to have ready

  • The Medicare card and Social Security number
  • Recent statements for bank accounts and investments
  • Social Security, pension and any other income amounts
  • The name of the Part D plan, if your parent already has one

If you are helping a parent apply, sit with them during the call or online application.

For free help, call HIICAP, New York's Medicare counseling program, at 1-800-701-0501. Say your county or borough and you will be routed to your local HIICAP program.

How does Extra Help work with EPIC?

EPIC is New York State's own drug program for people 65 and older with income up to $75,000 (single) or $100,000 (married). It sits on top of Part D. Extra Help and EPIC are designed to work together.

  • EPIC requires income-eligible members to apply for Extra Help. The EPIC application doubles as an Extra Help application.
  • No EPIC fees. The state says members approved for Extra Help, a Medicare Savings Program or Medicaid spenddown pay no EPIC fees.
  • Lower copays. Members with Extra Help get lower EPIC copayments than the standard $3 to $20.
  • Premium help. For Extra Help members in enhanced or Medicare Advantage plans, EPIC can help with premiums up to the basic amount, after Medicare's subsidy.
  • A path to MSP. EPIC sends applications to New York Medicaid to check for a Medicare Savings Program, which pays the Part B premium too.

Our EPIC guide covers the Fee and Deductible Plans in full.

Is it different in New York City?

Extra Help itself is federal, so the rules are the same in Manhattan or Montauk. The difference is the automatic route. In the five boroughs, HRA handles Medicare Savings Program and Medicaid applications for people 65 and older. Call the HRA Medicaid Helpline at 1-888-692-6116 or apply online through ACCESS HRA. Outside NYC, your county Department of Social Services handles those applications. The New York Medicaid Helpline is 1-800-541-2831.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Assuming savings rule your parent out. They may block direct Extra Help, but not the New York Medicare Savings Program route.
  • Skipping Part D. Extra Help pays toward a Part D plan. Without one, there is nothing to apply it to.
  • Picking a pricey plan without checking. A premium above the basic amount may not be fully covered. A HIICAP counselor can compare plans during fall open enrollment, October 15 to December 7.
  • Ignoring letters. Social Security, Medicare and the state all send notices about Extra Help status. Read them and keep them with your Medicare papers.
  • Not combining with EPIC. For people 65 and older, EPIC on top of Extra Help can bring costs down further.

For the full list of 2027 Medicare numbers, see our 2027 Medicare costs guide.

faq.q: How do I get Extra Help for my mom in the Bronx if she has savings?
faq.a: Apply to HRA for the Medicare Savings Program. New York does not count savings for it, and people who qualify get Extra Help automatically. Call the HRA Medicaid Helpline at 1-888-692-6116.

faq.q: My dad in Syracuse just got EPIC. Does he still need Extra Help?
faq.a: Yes, if his income is low enough. EPIC requires income-eligible members to apply, and Extra Help members pay no EPIC fees and get lower EPIC copays.

faq.q: What are the Extra Help copays for 2027?
faq.a: Medicare says up to $5.80 for each generic drug and up to $14.40 for each brand-name drug, with a $0 deductible. After drug costs reach $2,400, you pay $0 for covered drugs.

faq.q: What are the Extra Help income limits?
faq.a: For 2026, Medicare lists $23,940 in yearly income and $18,090 in resources for a single person, and $32,460 and $36,100 for a married couple.

faq.q: Do I get Extra Help automatically?
faq.a: Yes, if you get full Medicaid, a Medicare Savings Program, or SSI. Otherwise, apply through Social Security online or at 1-800-772-1213.

faq.q: Can I apply for Extra Help any time?
faq.a: Yes. Social Security says you can apply for Extra Help any time, before or after you enroll in Part D.

title: Free and discounted things for older New Yorkers
seoTitle: Free and Discounted Things for NY Seniors 62 and Up
seoDesc: Free state park entry on weekdays at 62, half-price MTA fares at 65, $5 fishing licenses at 70, an $80 lifetime national parks pass and NYC museum deals.
dek: Turning 62, 65 and 70 in New York opens up real savings. Here are the free state park days, half-price transit, cheap hunting and fishing licenses, federal park passes, train discounts and free museum options, with the official rules for each.
keyFacts: State parks: free vehicle entry on non-holiday weekdays at 62+
MTA reduced fare at 65+: $1.50 subway and local bus
NY fishing, hunting and trapping licenses: $5 each at 70+
National parks Senior Pass at 62+: $20 a year or $80 for life
Amtrak: 10% off most fares at 65+
body:
Older New Yorkers can get into most state parks free on weekdays starting at 62, ride the subway and local buses for half price at 65, and buy fishing and hunting licenses for $5 at 70. Add a federal park pass, an Amtrak discount and free NYC museum options, and the savings add up quickly.

Most of these perks need nothing more than an ID card. A few need a short application. This guide lists each one by age, with the exact rules from the agency that runs it, so you or your parent can start using them this week.

What can I get at each age?

AgeBenefitCost
62+Golden Park Program, NY State ParksFree vehicle entry, non-holiday weekdays
62+America the Beautiful Senior Pass (federal lands)$20 a year or $80 for life
65+MTA reduced fare, subway and local bus$1.50 a ride
65+LIRR and Metro-North senior fareUp to 50% off the peak one-way fare
65+Amtrak senior discount10% off most fares
65+Metropolitan Museum of Art senior ticket$22 (NY residents can pay what they wish)
70+NY fishing, hunting and trapping licenses$5 each

How do free state park days work at 62?

The Golden Park Program gives New York residents 62 and older free vehicle entry to most state parks, boat launch sites and arboretums. It works Monday through Friday, except holidays. You do not apply. At the gate, show a valid New York State driver license or non-driver ID card. That card is the pass.

At state historic sites and state-run golf courses, the program gives a reduced fee instead of free entry. A few places are left out of the free vehicle access, including Walkway Over the Hudson, Artpark, Lake Superior State Park, Fahnestock Winter Park, Mark Twain State Park, Soaring Eagles Golf Course and Ganondagan State Historic Site.

For weekends and holidays, State Parks sells the Empire Pass in one-season, multi-season and lifetime versions at its online store. New York residents with disabilities can get the Access Pass, and veterans and Gold Star families can get the Lifetime Liberty Pass. Questions go to State Parks at 518-474-0456.

A New York driver license is all you need for free weekday park entry at 62.

How do I get half-price MTA fares?

Anyone 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, can get MTA reduced fare. Qualifying disabilities include getting Medicare for a reason other than age, blindness, deafness, or a cognitive or ambulatory disability. Subway rides, the Staten Island Railway, and local, limited and Select Bus Service cost $1.50 at all times. Reduced-fare express bus rides cost $3.60, except during weekday rush hours (6 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m.).

Reduced fare riders can tap with a Reduced-Fare OMNY card. After 12 paid rides in seven days, the rest of that week's rides are free. For a full walkthrough, see our MTA reduced fare guide.

  1. Go in person for speed. Visit an MTA Customer Service Center at select subway stations, the center at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan on weekdays, or a Mobile Sales van. Seniors 65 and older can often get a card the same day, though some applications need more review.
  2. Or apply by mail. Send the application, a passport-style photo (2 by 1.5 inches) and a copy of your ID to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625. Mail can take up to three months.
  3. Load and ride. Tap the Reduced-Fare OMNY card at the turnstile or fare reader. The 12-ride weekly cap applies automatically.
  4. Get help. OMNY customer service is 877-789-6669, any time.

What about the LIRR and Metro-North?

Riders 65 and older, people with disabilities and Medicare recipients save up to 50% off the full one-way peak fare. The tickets work on all trains and can be bought onboard without the usual surcharge. Show a driver license, non-driver ID, passport, NYC Aging ID, or a Reduced-Fare OMNY card or MetroCard. A Medicare card works only with a separate photo ID.

If your parent can no longer manage buses or the subway, look at Access-A-Ride paratransit in the five boroughs.

Are hunting and fishing licenses cheaper at 70?

Yes. New York residents 70 and older pay $5 each for a fishing, hunting or trapping license. Bowhunting and muzzleloading privileges are free, but you still need the $5 base hunting license. To hunt or trap, you need a hunter education certificate or a past license. Buy from any license issuing agent or through the state's online and phone system (DECALS), and be ready to show proof of New York residency.

Which federal passes and travel discounts can I use?

National parks Senior Pass

U.S. citizens and permanent residents 62 and older can buy the America the Beautiful Senior Pass. It costs $20 for one year or $80 for life. It covers entrance fees at national parks and other federal recreation sites and can cut some amenity fees, such as camping, by 50%.

Buy it in person at a federal recreation site, online from the USGS store (mail can take up to three weeks), or as a digital pass on Recreation.gov that works right away. You need proof of age and citizenship or residency, so it cannot be bought as a gift. Bring photo ID each time you use it. Passes cannot be refunded, transferred or replaced if lost, so keep it somewhere safe. People who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents cannot buy the Senior Pass.

Amtrak

Travelers 65 and older get 10% off most rail fares on most Amtrak trains. Pick "Senior" as the traveler type when booking. Sleeping car charges are not discounted, and the discount cannot be combined with other offers. Carry proof of age on the train. On cross-border trains run with VIA Rail Canada, the senior age is 60.

What free museum and library deals are there in New York City?

IDNYC

IDNYC is New York City's free ID card for residents 10 and older. It is free for anyone who applies through December 31, 2026. It works as a library card and is accepted as ID by police and City agencies. Book an appointment online or through 311. Some enrollment centers take walk-ins on certain weekdays. You need documents worth 3 points of identity and 1 point of New York City residency, and the IDNYC Document Calculator shows what each paper is worth. Cards issued to people 16 and older last five years.

Cardholders can get a free one-year membership or discounted tickets at a list of cultural institutions. The list includes the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the American Museum of Natural History, the Museum of Modern Art, Lincoln Center, the Bronx Zoo, the Queens Museum, the Brooklyn Academy of Music and the Staten Island Museum. If you redeemed a free membership or paid for one there in the last five years, you are not eligible at that institution. Some places set their own age limits. The Met's free membership, for example, is for cardholders 18 and older.

Culture Pass

Culture Pass lets cardholders of the Brooklyn, New York and Queens public libraries reserve free admission to more than 100 NYC cultural institutions, including museums, historical societies and public gardens. Go to culturepass.nyc, choose your library system and sign in with your library card. It is open to cardholders 13 and older, so it also works for an outing with a grandchild.

The Met

General admission is $22 for visitors 65 and older. New York State residents can pay what they wish instead, with a one-cent minimum, by showing an ID such as a New York driver license.

What other savings should older New Yorkers check?

  • Farmers market coupons. Low-income New Yorkers 60 and older can get a $25 coupon booklet each summer. See our SNAP guide for details.
  • Property tax breaks. Homeowners can save through Enhanced STAR and the senior citizen homeowners' exemption.
  • Rent freezes in NYC. Eligible tenants can lock in their rent with SCRIE or DRIE.
  • Heating help. HEAP helps with winter energy bills.
  • Prescription help. EPIC lowers drug costs for people 65 and older.

How do I make sure a discount actually works?

A simple routine before any outing

Carry a New York driver license or non-driver ID, since it is the proof for Golden Park, the Met's resident price and most senior fares. Check the official page the day before, because exceptions and hours change. Ask at the ticket window, since many discounts are not applied unless you request them.

If you help a parent who no longer drives, a non-driver ID from the DMV keeps these perks working. With it, they can still use the Golden Park Program on a ride with a friend, buy LIRR or Metro-North senior tickets and get in to the Met at the resident price.

Before you go anywhere, check the official page linked in our sources. Prices and rules can change, and a two-minute check saves a wasted trip.

faq.q: Can my mom get into state parks on Long Island free because she is over 62?
faq.a: On non-holiday weekdays, yes at most parks. The Golden Park Program gives New York residents 62 and older free vehicle entry to most state parks. She shows her New York driver license or non-driver ID at the gate. A short list of sites is excluded, so check the Golden Park page first.

faq.q: How does my dad in the Bronx get a senior MetroCard or OMNY card?
faq.a: He can get a Reduced-Fare card at 65. The fastest way is an MTA Customer Service Center or Mobile Sales van, where seniors may get a card the same day. He can also mail the application with a photo and ID copy, which can take up to three months.

faq.q: How much is the MTA senior fare?
faq.a: Reduced fare is $1.50 for the subway, Staten Island Railway and local, limited and Select buses. Express buses are $3.60 outside weekday rush hours.

faq.q: At what age is a New York fishing license $5?
faq.a: New York residents 70 and older pay $5 for a fishing, hunting or trapping license. Bowhunting and muzzleloading privileges are free with the $5 base hunting license.

faq.q: How much is the national parks senior pass?
faq.a: U.S. citizens and permanent residents 62 and older pay $20 for an annual Senior Pass or $80 for a lifetime pass. It covers entrance fees at federal recreation sites.

faq.q: Does Amtrak have a senior discount?
faq.a: Yes. Travelers 65 and older get 10% off most fares on most trains. Sleeping accommodations are not discounted, and you need proof of age when buying and onboard.

title: HEAP in New York for 2026 to 2027: heating help for older adults
seoTitle: HEAP NY 2026-2027: Income Limits, Dates, How to Apply
seoDesc: New York HEAP for 2026 to 2027: income limits, the $990 fuel benefit, emergency help from January 4, 2027, furnace repair, and utility and phone discounts.
dek: New York's Home Energy Assistance Program opened November 2, 2026 and can pay up to $1,086 toward heat. Households with someone 60 or older get extra. Here is who qualifies, how to apply in NYC and the rest of the state, and the utility discounts that come with it.
keyFacts: Regular HEAP opened November 2, 2026; Emergency HEAP opens January 4, 2027
Income limit: $3,563 a month for one person, $4,659 for two
Up to $1,086 for the Regular benefit, including add-ons
Extra $35 when the household includes someone 60 or older
HEAP households get the utility Energy Affordability discount automatically
body:
HEAP (the Home Energy Assistance Program) helps New York households with low and moderate incomes pay for heat, and the 2026 to 2027 Regular benefit opened on November 2, 2026. Eligible households can get up to $1,086, depending on how they heat and their income, and an older adult in the home adds to the amount.

HEAP is more than one check. There is a Regular benefit once a season, an Emergency benefit if the heat is about to be cut off or the tank is nearly empty, help to fix or replace a broken furnace, and cooling help in summer. Getting HEAP also signs a household up for a monthly discount on gas and electric bills. In New York City, the Human Resources Administration (HRA) runs HEAP. Everywhere else, it is the county Department of Social Services (DSS).

Who qualifies for HEAP this season?

A household can qualify by income, or by already receiving certain benefits. The state lists these rules:

  • Every household member is a U.S. citizen, a U.S. non-citizen national or a qualified non-citizen, and gives a valid Social Security number.
  • The household receives SNAP, Temporary Assistance or SSI (HRA lists Code A SSI, for people living alone), or its gross monthly income is at or below the limit below.
  • Having money in the bank, stocks, bonds or other resources does not by itself rule a household out of the Regular benefit.
Household size2026 to 2027 maximum gross monthly income
1$3,563
2$4,659
3$5,756
4$6,852
5$7,948
6$9,045
Each additional person (after 13)Add $710

Some households receive Regular HEAP automatically, and the state says households that are not automatically enrolled can apply. If your parent gets SNAP or Temporary Assistance, ask the local office whether a benefit was already issued before filing a new application.

Say your mom lives alone in a house near Utica, heats with oil and gets $2,100 a month from Social Security and a small pension. She is under the $3,563 limit for one person, so she can apply for the Regular benefit. Because she is over 60, the household counts as having a vulnerable member and her benefit includes the extra $35.

How much does HEAP pay?

Benefit2026 to 2027 amount
Regular, oil, kerosene or propane$990 base (up $90 from last season)
Regular, wood, pellets or coal$700 base (up $65)
Add-on for lower incomes$61 for direct-pay heat households at or below 130% of the federal poverty level
Add-on for a vulnerable member$35 if someone is 60 or older, under 6, or permanently disabled
Most a Regular benefit can reach$1,086

Households that pay for natural gas or electric heat, or whose heat is included in the rent, get different amounts. There is one Regular benefit per season. The state notifies applicants within 30 business days after the local office receives the application.

A household member who is 60 or older adds $35 to the Regular benefit and loosens the savings limit for Emergency HEAP.

What if the heat is about to run out?

Emergency HEAP opens January 4, 2027. It is for households at risk of running out of heating fuel or having a utility shut off. HRA says households can have resources under $2,500, or under $3,750 if someone in the home is 60 or older or under 6. In New York City, apply for an emergency benefit by phone at 718-557-1399 or in person. Outside the city, call your county DSS.

If your parent has no heat in cold weather, do not wait for a HEAP decision. Call the HEAP emergency line or county DSS the same day, and call the utility to explain the situation. In the city, 311 can also connect you to help.

Can HEAP fix a broken furnace or boiler?

Yes, for homeowners. HEAP Heating Equipment Repair and Replacement (HERR) opened October 1, 2026. It helps homeowners whose primary heating equipment does not work. HRA lists up to $4,000 for a repair or $8,000 for a replacement, based on actual cost, and a household can use it once every ten years.

Clean and Tune pays for a professional to inspect and clean the main heating system, up to $500 based on actual cost. HRA and Westchester County list it as open for the 2026 to 2027 season as of October 1, 2026. Ask your local office whether funds are available where your parent lives.

Apply for both through HRA in the city or your county DSS. Never pay a stranger who knocks on the door claiming to be from HEAP.

Is there help with cooling in summer?

HEAP Cooling Assistance can pay for an air conditioner or fan, up to $800 with installation for a window or portable unit or a fan, or up to $1,000 for an existing wall sleeve unit. It opens in spring. Watch for the 2027 dates from HRA or your county DSS.

How do I apply in NYC and the rest of the state?

  1. See if your parent already gets it. Some households get Regular HEAP without applying. Ask the HEAP office before filing.
  2. Gather papers. Have proof of where your parent lives, recent proof of income for everyone in the home, photo ID or other identification and a Social Security number for each person, plus the heating or utility account details. The application lists anything else your office needs.
  3. Apply in New York City. Online through ACCESS NYC (ACCESS HRA), in person at a HEAP office, or by mail to HRA/HEAP, PO Box 1401, Church Street Station, New York, NY 10008. Questions go to 718-557-1399.
  4. Apply outside New York City. Online at myBenefits.ny.gov, in person at your county DSS, or by printing the application and mailing it to your county HEAP office.
  5. Ask for help filling it out. Older adults can call their county Office for the Aging, or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.
  6. Watch the mail. Answer any request for more papers quickly so the application does not close.

The state OTDA hotline is 1-800-342-3009, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The state pays benefits on a first-come, first-served basis, so apply early.

What mistakes hold up a HEAP application?

  • Waiting until the coldest week. The state pays benefits first come, first served. Apply in November or December if you can.
  • Counting net instead of gross income. The limits use gross monthly income, so use the amount before anything is taken out. For Social Security, that means the benefit before the Medicare premium is deducted.
  • Leaving someone out. Everyone in the household counts toward the household size and the income. A spouse in a nursing home or an adult child who stays part of the year can change the numbers, so ask the HEAP office how to list them.
  • Applying twice. A parent who already got HEAP automatically does not need to apply again, and there is one Regular benefit per season.
  • Ignoring the mail. If the office asks for a missing paper and gets no answer, the application can be closed. Keep an eye on the mailbox for a few weeks after applying, or set up an online account so notices are easier to see.
  • Trusting door-to-door offers. Be wary of anyone who knocks offering HEAP-paid furnace work. HERR requests go through your HEAP office.

Say your dad lives alone in a Riverdale apartment where heat is included in the rent. He can still apply. Households with heat included in the rent get a smaller benefit, and getting HEAP at any amount enrolls him in the Energy Affordability Program discount on his electric bill.

What other utility and phone discounts can older adults get?

Energy Affordability Program (EAP)

EAP is a monthly discount on gas and electric bills from New York's large utilities, including Con Edison, National Grid, NYSEG, RG&E, Central Hudson, National Fuel, Orange & Rockland and PSEG Long Island. Since January 2026 it covers households below state median income, or below area median income in New York City, Westchester, Suffolk and Nassau. The governor's office says it can save households up to $500 a year.

Household sizeCon Edison and National Grid NYCNational Grid Long IslandUpstate and all other NY utilities
1$113,400$115,450$69,477
2$129,600$131,950$90,854
3$145,800$148,450$112,232

The governor's office says households that get HEAP or Public Assistance are enrolled automatically. People on SNAP, Medicaid or SSI are not, because of privacy rules, so they need to enroll through their utility. The Department of Public Service also lists a veterans disability or survivors pension, Lifeline and federal public housing assistance as qualifying programs. Anyone who qualifies by income alone can apply at ny.gov/EAP. Utilities must also place EAP customers on budget billing, which spreads costs evenly over the year. You can opt out by calling the utility.

Lifeline phone and internet discount

The federal Lifeline program takes up to $9.25 a month off phone, internet or bundled service. You qualify with income at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, or by receiving SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal public housing assistance or the Veterans and Survivors Pension. Only one Lifeline benefit is allowed per household. Apply through the FCC's National Verifier or through a participating phone company, or call the Lifeline Support Center at 1-800-234-9473.

One application can lead to more help

A parent who qualifies for HEAP may also qualify for SNAP or help with Medicare costs. See our guides to SNAP for older New Yorkers and the Medicare Savings Program.

faq.q: When does HEAP open for 2026 to 2027?
faq.a: The Regular benefit opened November 2, 2026. Emergency HEAP opens January 4, 2027. HERR, the furnace repair and replacement benefit, opened October 1, 2026.

faq.q: What is the HEAP income limit for one person in New York?
faq.a: For the 2026 to 2027 season, a one-person household can have gross monthly income up to $3,563. For two people the limit is $4,659.

faq.q: How do I apply for HEAP for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Apply online through ACCESS NYC (ACCESS HRA), in person at an HRA HEAP office, or by mail to HRA/HEAP, PO Box 1401, Church Street Station, New York, NY 10008. Call 718-557-1399 with questions or for an emergency.

faq.q: My dad's furnace in Syracuse stopped working. Can HEAP help?
faq.a: If he owns the home, he can apply to Onondaga County DSS for HEAP Heating Equipment Repair and Replacement. HRA lists the benefit at up to $4,000 for a repair or $8,000 for a replacement, once every ten years.

faq.q: Do seniors get more from HEAP?
faq.a: Yes. A household with someone 60 or older gets an extra $35 on the Regular benefit, and Emergency HEAP allows up to $3,750 in resources instead of $2,500.

faq.q: Does HEAP lower my monthly electric bill too?
faq.a: HEAP households are automatically enrolled in the Energy Affordability Program, a monthly discount from New York's large gas and electric utilities that can save up to $500 a year.

title: Medicaid for New Yorkers 65 and older: 2026 limits and how to apply
seoTitle: NY Medicaid for Seniors: 2026 Income and Asset Limits
seoDesc: Medicaid for New Yorkers 65+: 2026 income and resource limits, home care vs nursing home rules, the 60-month lookback, MLTC, spenddown and where to apply.
dek: Medicaid pays for home care and nursing home care for many older New Yorkers. Here are the 2026 limits, the lookback, Managed Long Term Care, spenddown and where to apply.
keyFacts: 2026 income limit: $1,836 a month single, $2,489 couple
2026 resource limit: $33,038 single, $44,796 couple
60-month lookback for nursing home Medicaid
At-home spouse keeps up to $4,066.50 a month (2026)
NYC HRA Medicaid Helpline: 1-888-692-6116
body:
A New Yorker 65 or older can get Medicaid in 2026 with monthly income up to $1,836 ($2,489 for a couple) and resources up to $33,038 ($44,796 for a couple). If income is higher, New York's spenddown program and pooled trusts can still open the door, especially for home care.

Medicaid for older adults covers far more than doctor visits. It is the main way New Yorkers pay for long-term home care and nursing home care. The rules change if your mom or dad needs care at home instead of in a nursing home, and on where they live. In the five boroughs you deal with the city's Human Resources Administration (HRA). Everywhere else, you deal with the county Department of Social Services (DSS). This guide walks through the limits, the two kinds of Medicaid, the lookback, Managed Long Term Care and how to apply.

What are the 2026 income and resource limits?

These figures took effect January 1, 2026, and come from the state's Medicaid income and resource standards for people who are 65 or older, blind or disabled. The state also lets $20 of monthly unearned income go uncounted.

2026 Medicaid, age 65+SingleCouple
Monthly income limit$1,836$2,489
Monthly limit with the $20 disregard$1,856$2,509
Yearly income limit$22,025$29,864
Resource limit$33,038$44,796

The 2027 limits had not been published as of November 25, 2026. New York ties them to the federal poverty guidelines, which usually come out early in the year. In 2026 the state issued them on February 13, effective January 1. Until new figures are out, use the table above.

What if one spouse needs care?

When one spouse needs a nursing home or certain long-term care, New York protects the spouse who stays at home. For 2026, the at-home spouse can keep income up to $4,066.50 a month and resources of at least $74,820, up to $162,660, depending on the couple's assets. The state also sets a home equity limit of $1,130,000 for Medicaid to pay for nursing home and community-based long-term care.

Over the income limit is not the end of the road. Spenddown and pooled trusts exist for exactly that case.

What is the difference between community Medicaid and nursing home Medicaid?

Community Medicaid is Medicaid for people living at home, in their own place or with family. It pays for doctor and hospital care that Medicare does not, and it can pay for home care. That includes personal care aides, home health care, adult day health care and the Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (see our CDPAP guide). Most older New Yorkers on both Medicare and Medicaid who need long-term care at home get it through a Managed Long Term Care plan, explained below.

Nursing home Medicaid pays for a long-term stay in a nursing home once Medicare's short rehab coverage ends. The application looks deeper into your finances, and your income is budgeted toward the cost of care. HRA or the county tells you the monthly amount. A spouse at home keeps the protected amounts above.

Community MedicaidNursing home Medicaid
Where you liveAt home or with familyIn a nursing home
Lookback on gifts and transfersNone in effect (a proposed 30-month rule has not started)60 months
Long-term care delivered throughUsually a Managed Long Term Care planThe nursing home
If income is too highSpenddown or a pooled trustIncome is budgeted toward the cost of care

How does the lookback work for nursing home care?

Federal law requires a 60-month lookback for people applying for Medicaid nursing home care. Medicaid reviews money and property you gave away or sold for less than it was worth in the 60 months before the month you apply. A transfer like that can lead to a penalty period, when Medicaid will not pay for nursing home care.

In practice, this means a gift to a grandchild or putting a house in a child's name can delay coverage. Families often find this out at the worst moment, right after a hospital stay. Gather five years of bank statements early, and talk with an elder law attorney before moving any assets. You may read about a 30-month lookback for home care. New York proposed it in 2020, but the state delayed it and it is not in effect. Today the lookback applies to nursing home Medicaid.

What is Managed Long Term Care (MLTC)?

MLTC plans manage and pay for long-term care at home. The state requires people who have both Medicare and Medicaid, are 21 or older, and need community-based long-term care for more than 120 days to get it through an MLTC plan. Covered services include care management, home care, personal care, adult day health care, nursing home care, medical equipment, transportation, therapies and consumer directed personal assistance. Someone assessed as needing only Level 1 services does not qualify.

New York has three types of plans:

  • Partially capitated MLTC plans cover long-term care. Doctor and hospital care stay with Medicare and regular Medicaid.
  • PACE plans cover all of a member's care through one program. See our PACE guide.
  • Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) combines Medicare and Medicaid coverage in one plan.

How do I start MLTC?

Before joining a plan, your parent needs an assessment from the New York Independent Assessor. It includes a clinical appointment that takes up to an hour. To request an initial assessment, call the New York Independent Assessor helpline at 1-855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). If you are calling for a parent, you must be on file as their authorized representative.

What if my parent's income is over the limit?

New York has two tools for this.

Spenddown (excess income)

Spenddown works like a deductible. The amount your income is over the Medicaid limit is your "excess income." Once your medical bills in a month equal that amount, Medicaid pays covered bills for the rest of the month. You can also pay the excess straight to the county (a "pay-in") for a month when you need care. Bills can be paid or unpaid, and they can include doctor visits, prescriptions, transportation, copays and deductibles. Costs paid by EPIC count in full. Old unpaid medical bills can count, and paid bills from the three months before you applied can count too.

Say your dad in Utica has income $300 a month over the limit. A month when he has $300 in medical bills, or pays $300 to the county, is a month Medicaid covers. In New York City, you can fax bills to 917-639-0645 with your name, case and CIN numbers, your excess income amount and the months you want covered.

Pooled trusts

A pooled trust is run by a nonprofit and holds separate accounts for each member. The state says income placed in a pooled trust is not counted as income for Medicaid, as long as you can show it went into the trust. Pooled trusts are open to a certified disabled person of any age, so an older adult may need to be certified as disabled first. When the member dies, money the nonprofit does not keep goes to the state, up to what Medicaid paid. An elder law attorney or the trust itself can explain fees and setup. If your parent is married and in an MLTC plan, the state notes that income placed in a trust may still count, so ask first.

Where do I apply?

Where you apply depends on age, Medicare and where you live.

  1. In New York City, apply to HRA. HRA takes applications from residents 65 and older, people with disabilities or blindness, and people on Medicare. Apply online through ACCESS HRA, at a Medicaid office, or call the HRA Medicaid Helpline at 1-888-692-6116.
  2. Outside NYC, apply to your county DSS. Find your county's address and phone on the state's list of local social services offices. For example, Albany County DSS is 518-447-7492 and Erie County DSS is 716-858-8000.
  3. Some people use NY State of Health. Adults under 65 who are not on Medicare usually apply through NY State of Health or at 1-855-355-5777. That can apply to a younger spouse.
  4. Bring proof. HRA asks for proof of residency, identity, income and immigration status. For long-term care, expect to show bank and asset statements for the lookback period.
  5. Enroll in Medicare if you can. HRA requires people not yet enrolled in Medicare to sign up as a condition of eligibility.
  6. Read every notice. Answer requests for more papers by the date given. Missing a deadline is a common cause of denials.

The New York Medicaid Helpline is 1-800-541-2831. NY Connects can also help you sort out long-term care options in your county.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Giving money away before checking. Gifts within 60 months can delay nursing home coverage.
  • Assuming income is too high. Spenddown and pooled trusts exist for that case.
  • Missing the Medicare Savings Program. Even if your parent does not need full Medicaid, they may qualify for help with Medicare premiums, with no savings test. See our Medicare Savings Program guide.
  • Waiting for a crisis. Applications take time. Start when a hospital discharge planner first mentions home care or a nursing home.
  • Going it alone on big decisions. For a spouse at home or a family home, legal advice can protect a lot. Our power of attorney guide helps you get papers in order first.

faq.q: How do I get my dad on Medicaid for home care in Staten Island?
faq.a: Apply to HRA, which takes Medicaid applications from New York City residents 65 and older. Once he has Medicaid, call the New York Independent Assessor at 1-855-222-8350 to request the assessment needed to join a Managed Long Term Care plan.

faq.q: My mom in Westchester has too much income for Medicaid. Can she still get home care?
faq.a: Possibly. New York's spenddown program lets her qualify once her medical bills reach the amount she is over the limit, and a pooled trust can shelter excess income. Apply through Westchester County DSS at 914-995-3333.

faq.q: What is the Medicaid income limit for seniors in New York in 2026?
faq.a: $1,836 a month for a single person and $2,489 for a couple, or $1,856 and $2,509 counting the $20 disregard. The resource limit is $33,038 single and $44,796 for a couple.

faq.q: How far back does Medicaid look for nursing home care in New York?
faq.a: 60 months. Gifts or transfers for less than fair value in that period can cause a penalty period when Medicaid will not pay for nursing home care.

faq.q: Who must join a Managed Long Term Care plan?
faq.a: People with both Medicare and Medicaid who are 21 or older and need community-based long-term care for more than 120 days. Plans include partially capitated MLTC, PACE and Medicaid Advantage Plus.

faq.q: Have the 2027 Medicaid limits been released?
faq.a: Not as of November 25, 2026. New York ties the limits to the federal poverty guidelines, which usually come out early in the year.

title: Medicare Savings Program in New York: 2026 limits and how to apply
seoTitle: Medicare Savings Program NY: 2026 Income Limits
seoDesc: New York's Medicare Savings Program pays your Part B premium. See 2026 QMB and QI income limits, why there is no asset test, and how to apply in NYC or upstate.
dek: New York will pay your Medicare Part B premium if your income is under the limit, and it does not count your savings. Here are the 2026 limits, what QMB and QI pay, and where to apply.
keyFacts: QI income limit: $2,474 a month single, $3,355 couple (2026)
QMB income limit: $1,836 single, $2,489 couple (2026)
No savings or asset test for QMB or QI in New York
Part B premium paid: $209.40 a month in 2027
NYC HRA Medicaid Helpline: 1-888-692-6116
body:
The Medicare Savings Program (MSP) is how New York pays the Medicare Part B premium for people with modest incomes, and sometimes much more. In 2026 a single person in New York qualifies with monthly income up to $2,474 ($3,355 for a couple), and New York does not look at savings at all.

That last point surprises a lot of families. In New York, the state's own eligibility chart says there is no resource test for these programs. So your mom can have savings, a house and a car and still get help. The Part B premium is $202.90 a month in 2026 and goes up to $209.40 a month in 2027, so the savings come to more than $2,500 a year.

What does the Medicare Savings Program pay?

New York runs two Medicare Savings Programs for most people. Both are run by New York Medicaid, but they are separate from full Medicaid. You can get an MSP without being on Medicaid.

  • QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary). Pays your Medicare Part A and/or Part B premium. It also covers Medicare coinsurance and deductibles for Part A and Part B. In 2027 the Part B deductible is $292 and the Part A hospital deductible is $1,776, so QMB protects against big bills.
  • QI (Qualifying Individual, sometimes written QI-1). Pays the Part B premium only. You must have Medicare Part A. Funding is set each year, and HRA says the program is first come, first served. QI runs January 1 to December 31 each year.

You may see a third program, SLMB (Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary), on national websites. The New York State Department of Health's current MSP page lists only QMB and QI, and New York's QMB income limit already reaches 138% of the poverty level. If something you read mentions SLMB, apply anyway and let the state decide which program fits.

New York does not count savings for the Medicare Savings Program. Income is the only test.

What are the 2026 income limits in New York?

The limits are set as a percentage of the federal poverty level and took effect January 1, 2026. QMB goes up to 138% of poverty. QI covers incomes above 138% and up to 186%. The state shows each figure two ways, before and after $20 of monthly unearned income that is not counted.

ProgramSingle, monthlyCouple, monthlyWith $20 disregard (single / couple)Savings test
QMB$1,836$2,489$1,856 / $2,509None
QI$2,474$3,355$2,494 / $3,375None

HRA says income here means net income, your gross income minus allowable deductions and adjustments. Social Security, pensions, annuities and other regular income all count. The 2027 limits will be based on new federal poverty guidelines. Until the state publishes them, use the 2026 figures above.

A quick example

Say your dad lives alone in Schenectady and gets $2,300 a month from Social Security and a small pension. That is above the QMB line but under the QI line of $2,474. He would likely qualify for QI. The state would pay his Part B premium, which would no longer come out of his Social Security check. It does not matter that he has $40,000 in a savings account.

A couple example

Now say your parents live together in Hempstead on Long Island. Their combined Social Security and pensions come to $3,100 a month. The couple limit for QI is $3,355, so they are under it. The state would pay the Part B premium for each of them. At the 2027 premium of $209.40, that is $418.80 a month back in their checks, or $5,025.60 over a year. Their house and their savings play no part in the decision.

What if income is just over the line?

If your parent's income is above the QI limit, the MSP is off the table for now. But other programs reach further. EPIC, the state's drug program for people 65 and older, goes up to $75,000 in income for a single person. Medicaid has a spenddown program for people with high medical bills. Check again early each year, since the limits change when the federal poverty level is updated.

What else do I get with an MSP?

Getting a Medicare Savings Program also qualifies you for Extra Help, the federal program that lowers Part D drug costs. Medicare says so, and New York City's Human Resources Administration (HRA) says MSP members qualify automatically. That matters in New York because Extra Help on its own has a savings limit, but the MSP does not. For 2027, Medicare says people with Extra Help pay no more than $5.80 for generic drugs and $14.40 for brand-name drugs. Our Extra Help guide explains more.

MSP members who are also in EPIC pay no EPIC fees. See our EPIC guide for how the three programs stack.

How do I apply in New York City?

In the five boroughs, HRA takes Medicaid and MSP applications from people 65 and older and people on Medicare. You have two choices of application. One is a short form for MSP only. The other is a longer form that applies for both MSP and full Medicaid.

  1. Get the form. Apply online through ACCESS HRA, pick up a form at any HRA Community Medicaid Office, or call the HRA Medicaid Helpline at 1-888-692-6116 and ask for one.
  2. Gather proof. HRA asks for proof of residency, identity, income and immigration status. Bring your Medicare card and recent Social Security or pension statements.
  3. Send it to the right box. MSP only goes to HRA/Medical Assistance Program, Initial Eligibility Unit, 5th Fl., PO Box 24390, Brooklyn, NY 11202-9814. MSP plus Medicaid goes to HRA/Medical Assistance Program, MSP-CREP, 5th Fl., PO Box 24330, Brooklyn, NY 11202-9801.
  4. Keep copies. Photocopy everything and note the date you mailed it.
  5. Watch for the notice. HRA says QMB starts the first day of the month after you are found eligible. QI takes effect the month you apply.

What to have ready

  • Your Medicare card
  • Proof of identity and proof of where you live
  • Your latest Social Security benefit letter and any pension or annuity statements
  • Proof of immigration status, if it applies to you

If you use the longer form to apply for full Medicaid too, expect questions about savings, because full Medicaid has a resource limit.

How do I apply outside New York City?

Everywhere else in the state, you apply through your county Department of Social Services (DSS). The state's form is the DOH-4328, Medicare Savings Program Application, available in several languages on the Department of Health MSP page. The state says paper MSP applications must be mailed to the DSS in the county where you live. The same page also lists NY State of Health as a way to apply online.

Your county DSS phone number is on the state's list of local social services offices. A few examples:

CountyDepartment of Social Services
Albany518-447-7492
Erie (Buffalo)716-858-8000
Monroe (Rochester)585-753-2760
Westchester914-995-3333

General questions go to the New York Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831. For free one-on-one help with the form, call HIICAP, the state's Medicare counseling program, at 1-800-701-0501 and give your county.

What happens after I'm approved?

Once the state starts paying your Part B premium, it no longer comes out of your Social Security check, so your monthly deposit goes up. If the amount does not change after a few payments, call the agency that approved you. If you were approved for QMB, tell your doctors and hospitals. Medicare says providers are not allowed to bill QMB members for services and items Medicare covers, so show your QMB notice if a bill arrives.

Coverage is renewed over time. Read every letter from HRA or your county and answer by the date given, so your parent does not lose help over missing paperwork.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Assuming savings rule you out. In New York, savings do not count for QMB or QI.
  • Using gross income from memory. Pull the real numbers from a Social Security benefit letter. The $20 disregard and deductions can move someone under a line.
  • Applying for QI while on Medicaid. HRA notes you cannot get QI and other Medicaid at the same time. If your parent also needs Medicaid, use the longer form.
  • Not checking the Extra Help result. If your mom's pharmacy copays did not drop after approval, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).
  • Talking yourself out of it. Medicare's own advice is to apply even if you do not think you qualify.

If your parent's income is a little above the QI line, look at EPIC for drug costs and our 2027 Medicare costs guide for the full picture. If they need home care or a nursing home, read our Medicaid guide for New Yorkers 65 and older.

faq.q: How do I get the state to pay my mom's Medicare premium in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Apply to HRA for the Medicare Savings Program. You can apply online through ACCESS HRA, at a Community Medicaid Office, or by mail. In 2026 she qualifies with income up to $2,474 a month, and her savings do not count.

faq.q: My dad lives in Rochester and has $60,000 saved. Can he still get the Medicare Savings Program?
faq.a: Yes, if his income is under the limit. New York has no resource test for QMB or QI. He applies through the Monroe County Department of Social Services.

faq.q: Is there an asset limit for the Medicare Savings Program in New York?
faq.a: No. The state's income and resource chart lists no resource test for QMB or QI.

faq.q: Does the Medicare Savings Program give me Extra Help too?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare says people in a Medicare Savings Program also get Extra Help, and HRA says they qualify for it automatically.

faq.q: What happened to SLMB in New York?
faq.a: The state's current MSP page lists only QMB and QI. New York's QMB income limit reaches 138% of the poverty level. If you see SLMB mentioned, apply anyway and the state will check which program fits.

faq.q: When does the Medicare Savings Program start?
faq.a: In New York City, HRA says QMB starts the first day of the month after you are found eligible, and QI takes effect the month you apply.

title: How New York taxes retirement income
seoTitle: How New York Taxes Retirement Income and Pensions
seoDesc: New York does not tax Social Security or NY and federal government pensions, and lets people 59 1/2 and older exclude $20,000 of other pension and IRA income.
dek: New York is gentle on retirees. Social Security is not taxed, New York and federal government pensions are fully exempt, and most people 59½ or older can exclude up to $20,000 of other pension and IRA income. Here is how each piece works, plus a refundable credit for low-income households and where to get free help.
keyFacts: New York does not tax Social Security benefits
NY State, local and federal pensions are exempt at any age
Up to $20,000 of other pension and IRA income excluded at 59½
Real property tax credit: up to $375 if 65+, income $18,000 or less
NY personal income tax line: 518-457-5181
body:
New York does not tax Social Security, and it does not tax pensions from New York State, New York local governments or the federal government. On top of that, if you are 59½ or older, you can exclude up to $20,000 a year of other pension, annuity and IRA income from state tax.

For many retirees, that means little or no New York income tax. You still report this income on your federal return first, and New York starts from that federal number and then subtracts these items. This guide explains each one, shows how a married couple can use two exclusions, covers the small refundable real property tax credit for low-income households, and lists free places to get your return done.

Does New York tax Social Security?

No. Any Social Security benefits that are included in your federal adjusted gross income can be subtracted on your New York return. In plain terms, the part of Social Security the IRS taxes, New York takes back out.

You do not need to do anything special to get this. Tax software and volunteer preparers handle it on the subtraction lines of the New York return. Just make sure your SSA-1099 is included with your other forms.

Which pensions are fully exempt?

Pensions and distributions from these plans can be subtracted in full, at any age and in any form of payment:

  • New York State and local government plans, such as the state and New York City retirement systems and the New York State and New York City Teachers' Retirement Systems.
  • Federal government plans, including the military. For people in FERS, Thrift Savings Plan payouts count here too. The Tax Department says TSP payouts for CSRS participants go under the $20,000 exclusion instead.

This is a separate line from the $20,000 exclusion, and there is no dollar cap. A retired New York City teacher with a $60,000 pension pays no New York tax on that pension. If a government pension was rolled into an IRA, payouts generally stay fully excludable up to the amount rolled over.

Pensions from private employers do not qualify for this full exemption. The full exemption is limited to New York State, New York local and federal plans. Other pensions may still fit under the $20,000 exclusion below.

A New York State or federal pension is tax-free in New York at any age, with no dollar cap.

How does the $20,000 pension and annuity exclusion work?

If you were 59½ or older for the whole tax year, you can exclude up to $20,000 of qualifying pension and annuity income. If you turned 59½ during the year, only the money received after that date counts, still up to $20,000.

Income typeHow New York treats it
Social SecurityNot taxed
NY State, NYC and other NY local government pensionsFully exempt at any age
Federal and military pensionsFully exempt at any age
Private employer pension, periodic paymentsUp to $20,000 excluded at 59½ or older
IRA withdrawals, periodic or lump sumUp to $20,000 excluded at 59½, except money from contributions made after retiring
Periodic 401(k), 457 and employer 403(b) payoutsUp to $20,000 excluded at 59½
Annuity you bought with your own moneyDoes not qualify

What qualifies

The exclusion covers periodic payments for work you did as an employee before retiring. It also covers IRA payouts, both periodic and lump sum. Periodic payouts from 401(k) plans, 457 deferred compensation plans and 403(b) plans run by a corporation, foundation or public school count too. Keogh (HR-10) payouts can qualify. In each case, money that came from contributions made after you retired does not count.

What does not qualify

  • An annuity you bought on your own from an insurer or bank.
  • Payments you receive as a nonemployee spouse under a QDRO or New York domestic relations order. (If the plan is a New York or federal government plan, those payments can go on the government pension line instead.)
  • Employer contributions designated to a Roth account under the SECURE 2.0 Act.

Two spouses, two exclusions

Each spouse who has qualifying income can exclude up to $20,000 of their own income. That holds for joint and separate returns alike. But you cannot use any unused part of your spouse's exclusion.

Example: a couple in Albany

Say he is 68 with a $30,000 private company pension. She is 66 and takes $12,000 a year from her IRA. He excludes $20,000, and $10,000 of his pension stays taxable. She excludes all $12,000. Her unused $8,000 cannot be moved over to cover the rest of his pension.

Widows, widowers and heirs

If you get your own pension and a pension from a spouse who died, the Tax Department says you may claim up to $20,000 for each. A beneficiary of a deceased person's pension can claim the exclusion at any age if the person who died would have qualified. The total claimed by the person who died and all beneficiaries cannot top $20,000 a year, and it is shared among beneficiaries in proportion to what they inherited. If you also claim the disability income exclusion, the two together cannot top $20,000.

What is the real property tax credit?

The real property tax credit is a small refundable credit for very low-income homeowners and renters. You claim it on Form IT-214. If you are 65 or older (or your spouse or a dependent is), it can be worth up to $375. Otherwise the top is $75. If the credit is bigger than any tax you owe, New York sends the rest as a refund.

For tax year 2025, you must meet all of these:

  • Federal adjusted gross income of $18,000 or less (combined if married filing jointly).
  • You lived in the same New York home for at least six months and were a New York resident all year.
  • Nobody can claim you as a dependent.
  • All real property you own is worth $85,000 or less, and your home was not fully exempt from property taxes.
  • Renters paid average monthly rent of $450 or less. Heat, gas, electricity, furnishings and board do not count toward that.

You do not have to file a regular return to get it. You can file Form IT-214 by itself. Late claims are allowed. A 2025 claim can be filed until April 16, 2029. The 2023 deadline is April 15, 2027, and 2024 claims are due by April 17, 2028.

Homeowners should also check the school tax break in our STAR and Enhanced STAR guide and the local senior citizen homeowners' exemption. NYC renters can look at SCRIE, which freezes rent for eligible tenants.

Where can I get free tax help in New York?

Retirees have several free options, many staffed by trained volunteers who know the New York pension rules.

  • TCE and AARP Tax-Aide. The IRS Tax Counseling program serves people 60 and older and focuses on pension and retirement questions. Most of these sites are run by AARP Foundation Tax-Aide. Find one from January to April with the AARP site locator or by calling 888-227-7669.
  • VITA. The IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance program has no program-wide income limit, but many sites serve people who generally make about $70,244 or less. Find a VITA or TCE site at 800-906-9887.
  • The New York Tax Department's TAP program. In the 2026 season, it offered free guided filing at 47 in-person and virtual sites for people with federal adjusted gross income of $89,000 or less and investment income of $11,950 or less. Check the TAP page for next season.
  • Phone help. The Tax Department's personal income tax line is 518-457-5181, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  1. Collect the year's forms. SSA-1099 for Social Security, 1099-R for each pension, IRA or annuity, and any 1099-INT or 1099-DIV.
  2. Sort pensions into two piles. NY State, local and federal pensions go on the government line. Private pensions and IRA payouts go toward the $20,000 exclusion.
  3. Check each spouse separately. Each person gets their own $20,000. Make sure both are claimed if both qualify.
  4. Look at Form IT-214. If income is $18,000 or less, see whether the real property tax credit applies, even with no return due.
  5. Book free help early. TCE, AARP Tax-Aide and VITA sites fill up in February and March.
  6. Keep copies. Save the return and every 1099 for at least the years you might need to amend or claim a late credit.

What mistakes do New York retirees make?

  • Putting a government pension on the wrong line. A NY State, local or federal pension belongs on the government pension line, which has no cap. If it lands under the $20,000 exclusion, you may pay tax you do not owe.
  • Missing a spouse's exclusion. Each spouse with qualifying income gets $20,000.
  • Assuming a bought annuity counts. One purchased with your own money does not qualify.
  • Skipping IT-214. Very low-income older adults often do not file and leave up to $375 behind.
  • Forgetting the 59½ date. In the year you turn 59½, only income after that date counts.

One more point for people still working part time. Wages are taxed normally in New York at any age. The $20,000 exclusion and the government pension subtraction apply only to retirement income. A paycheck does not qualify.

Estate planning is a separate question. For that, see our guide to the New York estate tax. For how your Social Security check changes in 2027, see Social Security in 2027.

faq.q: Does New York State tax my dad's pension if he retired from a city job in Queens?
faq.a: No. Pensions from New York State and local government plans, including New York City retirement systems, are fully exempt from New York income tax at any age, with no dollar limit.

faq.q: My mom in Buffalo takes money from her IRA. Is it taxed by New York?
faq.a: If she is 59½ or older, up to $20,000 a year of IRA withdrawals can be excluded from New York tax. Money from contributions she made after retiring does not count, and any amount above $20,000 is taxable.

faq.q: Does New York tax Social Security?
faq.a: No. Social Security benefits included in federal adjusted gross income are subtracted on the New York return, so they are not taxed by the state.

faq.q: Can a married couple exclude $40,000 of pension income in New York?
faq.a: Yes, if each spouse is 59½ or older and each has at least $20,000 of their own qualifying pension, annuity or IRA income. One spouse cannot use the other's unused exclusion.

faq.q: Are federal and military pensions taxed in New York?
faq.a: No. Pensions from federal government plans, including the military, are fully exempt from New York income tax, separate from the $20,000 exclusion.

faq.q: Who can get the New York real property tax credit?
faq.a: For tax year 2025, full-year New York residents with federal adjusted gross income of $18,000 or less who lived in the same home for six months, owning property worth $85,000 or less or paying rent of $450 a month or less. It is worth up to $375 if someone in the household is 65 or older.
