title: SCRIE and DRIE: how the NYC rent freeze works for older adults
seoTitle: SCRIE and DRIE NYC Rent Freeze: Who Qualifies
seoDesc: NYC's SCRIE and DRIE rent freeze programs: the new $75,000 income limit, the one-third rent rule, which apartments qualify, how to apply and how to renew.
dek: New York City can freeze the rent of tenants 62 and older, and of tenants with disabilities, in rent-regulated apartments. The income limit just rose to $75,000. Here is how it works and how to sign up.
keyFacts: SCRIE is for tenants 62+; DRIE is for tenants 18+ with a disability award
Income limit raised from $50,000 to $75,000
Rent must be more than one-third of household income
Apply online through NYC TAP or on paper
Questions: call 311 (212-639-9675 from outside NYC)
body:
SCRIE (the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption) and DRIE (the Disability Rent Increase Exemption) freeze the rent of qualifying New York City tenants so future increases do not land on them. Together the city calls them the Rent Freeze Program, and the household income limit has risen from $50,000 to $75,000.

The landlord still collects the full legal rent. The difference between what you pay and the actual rent comes to the landlord as a property tax credit from the city. The longer your mom or dad stays in the program and keeps renewing, the more it is worth, because each new rent increase is covered. This guide explains who qualifies, which apartments count, how to apply through the Department of Finance (DOF) or the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD), and how to keep the benefit going.

Who qualifies for SCRIE and DRIE?

SCRIEDRIE
Age62 or older18 or older
Household incomeUp to $75,000 a year (raised from $50,000)
Rent burdenRent must be more than one-third of monthly household income
LeaseYou must live in the apartment and be named on the lease or rental agreement
Disability proofNot neededAn award of SSI, SSDI, a VA disability pension or compensation, or disability-related Medicaid if you received SSI or SSDI in the past

What changed with the income limit?

The Rent Freeze Program home page says the annual household income threshold has increased from $50,000 to $75,000, and the program's FAQ, revised November 19, 2026, uses the $75,000 limit. In testimony to the City Council on September 18, 2026, Finance said the state budget authorized the higher limit beginning July 1, 2026, and projected enrollment would grow by about 5,000 households. Some city pages, including the program's eligibility page, still show $50,000 as of late November 2026. Do not let an old page or form talk your parent out of applying.

If your parent applied after July 1, 2026 and was denied because of income, the city says it will review the application under the new limit. The same goes for a renewal denied for income after a benefit expired on June 30, 2026.

How is income counted?

Income is the combined income of everyone in the household for the previous calendar year. Finance may base it on federal adjusted gross income, and IRA distributions included in that figure can be subtracted. The program's FAQ lists items that are not counted, such as cash gifts, inheritances, energy assistance payments and SNAP benefits. People who got the benefit before July 1, 2024 may use an older method of counting income.

To test the one-third rule, divide annual household income by 36. Say your dad lives alone in a rent-stabilized one-bedroom in Jackson Heights, gets $34,200 a year from Social Security and a small pension, and pays $1,250 a month. One-third of his monthly income is $34,200 divided by 36, or $950. His rent is above that, so he meets the rent test, and his income is well under the limit.

Which apartments qualify?

The apartment type matters as much as age and income.

  • SCRIE: rent-controlled, rent-regulated and rent-stabilized apartments, plus certain Battery Park City and former Mitchell-Lama properties. SCRIE is also available in Mitchell-Lama and HDFC (Housing Development Fund Corporation) buildings, but those applications go through HPD.
  • DRIE: rent-controlled, rent-regulated and rent-stabilized apartments, Mitchell-Lama, Section 236 and HDFC apartments, plus certain Battery Park City and former Mitchell-Lama properties. DRIE applications go to Finance for every building type.

If the apartment is not on these lists, it does not qualify. For lease problems in a rent-regulated apartment, such as a landlord who will not give a renewal lease, contact the state Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR).

Divide yearly household income by 36. If the rent is higher than that number, the rent test is met.

How is the frozen rent set?

Your frozen rent is generally the higher of two amounts: the rent in your immediately prior lease, or one-third of your monthly income. New applicants whose lease shows a lower preferential rent may have the freeze based on that lower amount.

Major capital improvement (MCI) increases have their own rule. If the MCI order was issued within 90 days of your first application, the program covers that increase. If it was issued earlier, you pay it and it is added to your frozen rent.

The city says the benefit grows the longer you stay in the program, as long as you renew and stay eligible.

How do I apply?

Finance says online applications are processed faster. Apply through the NYC Tenant Access Portal (NYC TAP), or download the paper SCRIE or DRIE application from the Rent Freeze Program site. The city says translations of the paper applications will be available soon.

  1. Check the basics first. Confirm the apartment type, the age rule and the one-third rent test. If a city page still shows the old $50,000 limit, go by the $75,000 figure on the program's home page.
  2. Gather proof of age. A copy of one document such as a birth certificate, U.S. passport, driver's license, non-driver ID or a baptismal record.
  3. Gather proof of income for everyone in the household. Federal and state tax returns, W-2 forms and Social Security benefit statements, plus anything else the application lists. Include a signed letter from any boarder or relative who helps with rent.
  4. Gather rent papers. For a rent-stabilized apartment, send the prior and current leases signed by you and the landlord, plus any preferential rent rider or MCI order. For rent-controlled, send the RN 26 and RA33.10 forms for the prior and current year.
  5. For DRIE, add the award letter. The Notice of Award for SSI, SSDI, VA disability or disability-related Medicaid.
  6. Send copies only. Finance is clear: never send originals.
  7. Submit and keep a record. Save the confirmation from NYC TAP or make copies of everything you mail.

Applying in a Mitchell-Lama or HDFC building

For SCRIE in these buildings, contact HPD at 100 Gold Street, Room 7M, New York, NY 10038, or call 212-863-8494. Applications are also on nyc.gov/hpd. DRIE applicants in these buildings still apply with Finance.

What should families check before applying?

A little homework up front saves months of back and forth. Before your parent applies, walk through these points together.

  • Is the parent named on the lease? The program requires the applicant to live in the apartment and be named on the lease or rental agreement. If your mom has lived there for decades but the lease is only in your late father's name, sort that out with the landlord or DHCR first.
  • Who else lives there? Income counts for everyone in the household. A grown child who moved back in with a full-time job can push the household over $75,000. Money from a boarder or a relative who helps with rent counts too, and Finance asks for a signed letter about it.
  • Which year's income? Finance looks at the previous calendar year. A parent who retired last spring may still show a full year of wages on last year's return, and may qualify more easily the following year.
  • Are the leases on hand? For a rent-stabilized apartment, Finance needs both the prior and the current lease, signed by tenant and landlord. Ask the managing agent for copies early, since this is the piece that most often holds an application up.
  • Is a rent increase coming? The freeze covers future increases, so the sooner the application goes in, the more it protects. If an MCI order is on the way, filing within 90 days of it matters.

Say your parents, both in their late 60s, rent a rent-controlled apartment in Park Slope and had $61,000 in combined income last year from Social Security and part-time work. Under the old $50,000 limit they were shut out. Under the new $75,000 limit, they can apply if their rent is more than $61,000 divided by 36, or about $1,694 a month.

How do renewals work?

The benefit runs for a set period, one year or two depending on your benefit end date. Your approval order shows it. About 60 days before it ends, Finance mails a renewal application, and you can renew online in NYC TAP starting 60 days before expiration. The program's FAQ says the renewal must be filed within six months of the benefit expiration.

  • Shorter forms are available if you have been approved for at least five years in a row.
  • No renewal lease from the landlord? Use the Certification of No Renewal Lease form with proof that you live there. It cannot be used for consecutive renewal periods. For a landlord who will not provide a lease, contact DHCR.
  • Need more time because of a disability or illness? Call 311, write to Finance, or file the Request for an Extension of Time Due to a Disability or Physical or Mental Impairment. Medical documentation may be needed.

What happens if my parent moves or passes away?

Moving. The benefit can move to a new apartment. File an Apartment Benefit Transfer Application. The frozen rent may change based on the new apartment's legal rent.

A death or permanent move out. An eligible household member who was listed on an earlier application may take over the benefit. The FAQ says to file a Benefit Takeover Application within six months of the primary tenant's death or move, or within 90 days of a revocation notice, whichever is later. A surviving spouse or registered domestic partner who met the rules on the last application does not need a takeover application, but must send proof of the marriage or partnership.

Watch for rent freeze scams

Applying is free. No one from the city will ask for a fee to process SCRIE or DRIE. If a caller or visitor offers to speed things up for money, hang up and call 311 yourself.

Where can I get help in person?

Call 311 with any Rent Freeze question. From outside the city, or using TTY or relay, call 212-639-9675. You can visit the Finance Manhattan Assistance Center at 66 John Street, 3rd Floor. The city recommends booking an appointment first at nyc.gov/dofappointments. Mail goes to NYC Department of Finance, Rent Freeze Program, P.O. Box 3179, Union, NJ 07083.

If you disagree with a decision, the Rent Freeze ombudspersons at Finance can help sort it out once you have a written determination. They cannot check on a pending application.

Living outside the five boroughs? SCRIE and DRIE as described here are New York City programs. Ask your city or village housing office or county Office for the Aging if your community offers anything similar. Homeowners should look at the senior homeowners' exemption, and anyone struggling with heating bills should read our HEAP guide.

faq.q: What is the income limit for SCRIE now?
faq.a: The Rent Freeze Program home page says the household income threshold has increased from $50,000 to $75,000. Finance told the City Council the state budget authorized the higher limit beginning July 1, 2026.

faq.q: How do I get my mom's rent frozen in the Bronx?
faq.a: If she is 62 or older, lives in a rent-stabilized or rent-controlled apartment, has household income of $75,000 or less and pays more than one-third of her income in rent, apply for SCRIE online through NYC TAP or on paper. Call 311 with questions.

faq.q: My dad lives in a Mitchell-Lama building in Harlem. Where does he apply for SCRIE?
faq.a: SCRIE in Mitchell-Lama and HDFC buildings is handled by HPD at 100 Gold Street, Room 7M, or 212-863-8494. DRIE applicants in those buildings apply with the Department of Finance.

faq.q: What is the difference between SCRIE and DRIE?
faq.a: SCRIE is for tenants 62 and older. DRIE is for tenants 18 and older who receive SSI, SSDI, a VA disability pension or compensation, or disability-related Medicaid after past SSI or SSDI.

faq.q: How often do I renew SCRIE?
faq.a: Every one or two years, depending on your benefit period. Finance mails a renewal about 60 days before the benefit ends, and you can renew online in NYC TAP.

faq.q: What is the SCRIE phone number?
faq.a: Call 311. From outside New York City, or using TTY or relay, call 212-639-9675.

title: Westchester senior exemption limits by town and city
seoTitle: Westchester Senior Exemption Income Limits by Town
seoDesc: Westchester's RPTL 467 senior exemption by town and city: income limits, the county's $58,400 cap, Dec 1 and May 1 deadlines, RP-467 forms and assessor phones.
dek: Every Westchester city and town sets its own senior exemption limit and deadline. Here are the figures, forms and assessor phone numbers in one table.
keyFacts: Posted town and city schedules: 50% exemption up to about $50,000, sliding to $58,399.99
County tax line: $58,400 limit in Westchester County's 2025 senior benefits guide
White Plains deadline: December 1. New Rochelle: call to confirm (county calendar lists Dec 1)
Most towns: May 1. Eastchester, Mount Pleasant, New Castle: June 1
Some school districts stay lower, such as $37,400 in Yorktown and Peekskill
body:
In the Westchester cities and towns that post a full schedule, an owner 65 or older can get the full 50% senior exemption with income up to about $50,000, and a smaller cut on a sliding scale up to $58,399.99. Deadlines trip up many families, because Westchester does not run on one calendar. White Plains closes on December 1, most towns on May 1, and Eastchester, Mount Pleasant and New Castle on June 1. New Rochelle and Yonkers have their own dates, so call those assessors.

This exemption comes from Section 467 of the Real Property Tax Law. Each city, town, village, school district and the county picks its own limit, so one house can have three different limits on three different tax bills. The table below pulls the figures from each assessing unit's own page or adopted code, and the dates from the county's assessment calendar. Where a unit does not publish its limit, it says call the assessor.

Phone numbers come from each assessor's own page where one is posted, and otherwise from the County Clerk's list of municipal assessors. Codes can trail a newer local law, so call before you rely on a number. Several assessors post only one ceiling and do not post the full scale.

Do Westchester villages assess separately?

A few do, for village taxes only. The county's assessment calendar lists village rolls with a January 1 taxable status date for Buchanan, Bronxville, Larchmont, Mount Kisco, Pleasantville and Sleepy Hollow. Pleasantville says on its own site that the village offers its own senior exemption. In other villages the town assessor handles the application. For example, the Greenburgh assessor takes applications under Irvington's village law, and the Town of Rye assessor supplies the forms for Port Chester. If your parent lives in a village, ask both the village clerk and the town assessor whether one form covers every bill.

How does the 467 exemption work, and what is the state maximum?

The exemption cuts the taxable assessed value of the home by up to 50%. The state Tax Department sets the outer limits. Each locality picks a top income for the 50% level anywhere from $3,000 to $50,000. A locality that picks $50,000 may add a sliding scale with a 20% exemption below $55,700, 10% below $57,500 and 5% below $58,400. It may also give more than 50% to lower incomes, up to 65% under $47,000. None of the Westchester pages checked for this guide posts the 55% to 65% option.

The basic rules are the same everywhere.

  • Age. Each owner generally must be 65 or older. If the owners are spouses or siblings with a common parent, one owner at 65 is enough.
  • Ownership. Usually 12 consecutive months before filing, unless the owner had the exemption on a previous home.
  • Residence. The home must be the legal residence of all owners, with exceptions such as an owner receiving care in a nursing home.
  • School-age children. A child living in the home who attends public school generally blocks the exemption. Private or parochial school does not.

Which year's income counts?

Income starts with federal adjusted gross income, with changes set by the 2023 state law. Taxable IRA distributions come out, and Social Security left out of adjusted gross income goes back in, though a locality may opt out of either. Tax-exempt interest and dividends are added. Some places, such as New Rochelle, also subtract unreimbursed medical and prescription costs. The year depends on the taxable status date. If that date is on or after April 15, the latest calendar year counts. If it is before April 15, the year before that counts. Most Westchester towns use May 1 or June 1, so they use the latest year. Cortlandt, for example, asks for 2025 returns on 2026 applications. Village rolls dated January 1 fall before April 15, so ask the village which year it wants.

What is Westchester County's own limit, and do school districts differ?

The county limit applies to the county line of the tax bill. The county's own 2025 senior financial benefits guide lists the county income limit as $58,400. Assessor notices from Mount Kisco and Pound Ridge say a county local law raised it from $37,399 to $58,399, and Yorktown and Peekskill both list the county limit as income under $58,400. In May 2024 the County Executive also signed a law, passed unanimously by the Board of Legislators, that leaves Social Security out of the income count for the county exemption.

School districts set their own limits, and some are much lower. The Town of Yorktown lists less than $37,400 for the Yorktown, Croton and Ossining school districts and less than $50,000 for Lakeland. Peekskill lists less than $37,400 for city and school taxes. Cortlandt warns that school limits may differ from its town and county figure. So a parent can qualify on the county and town bill and still pay full school tax. Ask the assessor for the limit of each district on your parent's bill.

One house can carry three income limits: one for the town or city, one for the county and one for the school district.

How do I apply or renew in Westchester?

  1. Find the right office. Use the table above. In a village, check whether the village also assesses.
  2. Get the form. First-time applicants use Form RP-467. Renewals use Form RP-467-Rnw. If no one had to file a federal return, add the Form RP-467-Wkst income worksheet. Instructions are in Form RP-467-I on the Tax Department site.
  3. Gather proof. Bring proof of age and the full federal return for the year the assessor uses. Cortlandt asks for all pages and backup. The Town of Rye also asks for a copy of the deed and, if there is rental income, its own rental worksheet.
  4. File by the taxable status date. Hand it in or mail it so it arrives on time. Cortlandt says its May 1 date has no exceptions.
  5. Watch for the renewal. Greenburgh mails renewals from late December through January. Cortlandt mails them in late February and asks you to call if one has not arrived by the end of March. Rye Town and Greenburgh require a renewal every year.
  6. Bought after the deadline? The Tax Department says you can apply within 30 days of the purchase, and the assessor has 30 days to decide.

Can my parent get the senior exemption and Enhanced STAR?

Yes. The Tax Department says senior exemption recipients may also be eligible for the STAR exemption or credit, including Enhanced STAR. They are separate programs with separate rules, so signing up for one does not sign you up for the other.

Senior exemption (467)Enhanced STAR
AgeGenerally every owner 65 or older by the taxable status dateOne resident owner 65 or older by December 31
Income limitSet locally; the town and city schedules posted here top out at $58,399.99$110,750 for 2026 benefits, $113,550 for 2027
Which taxesEach line that adopted it (county, city or town, village, school)School taxes only
Where to applyLocal assessor, Form RP-467State Tax Department for the STAR credit (see our STAR guide)

Enhanced STAR uses a different income measure, adjusted gross income minus taxable IRA distributions, and looks back two years. Our full STAR guide covers the credit and the automatic upgrade.

What does this look like with real figures?

This is an illustration using posted figures, not a real household. Say your mom owns a house in Peekskill, lives alone, and her 2025 income counted under the 467 rules is $45,000. Peekskill's page lists under $58,400 for county tax and under $37,400 for city and school tax. She would qualify on the county bill but not on the city or school bills. Enhanced STAR counts income a different way, but if hers is also about $45,000, it is far below the $113,550 limit for 2027 benefits. So Enhanced STAR can still lower the school bill the senior exemption does not touch.

Now move the same $45,000 to New Rochelle. The city code gives 50% to income under $50,000, so the city tax line would get the full 50% exemption, provided she files on time. Confirm the date with the assessor, because the county calendar lists December 1 and the city code says May 1.

What mistakes cost Westchester families the exemption?

  • Missing a date that is not May 1. White Plains uses December 1, and the county calendar lists December 1 for New Rochelle too. Yonkers runs on its own calendar, so call the assessor at 914-377-6200.
  • Skipping a renewal. Missing one can mean a full bill the next year.
  • Reading one limit as the only limit. County, town and school limits can differ on the same bill.
  • Sending the wrong year's return. Ask which year the assessor wants before you copy anything.
  • Assuming a co-op qualifies everywhere. White Plains says co-op owners get the county tax exemption only.

For help beyond property taxes, see the Westchester County page and our statewide senior exemption guide.

title: The senior citizens homeowners' exemption in New York and NYC
seoTitle: Senior Homeowners' Exemption NY and NYC SCHE Guide
seoDesc: How New York's senior citizens exemption and NYC's SCHE cut property taxes by up to 50%: the $58,399 income scale, local options, March deadlines and renewals.
dek: New York lets towns, cities, counties and school districts cut the taxable value of a senior's home by up to half. In New York City the program is called SCHE. Here is how the income scale works and how to apply.
keyFacts: Cuts a home's taxable assessment by up to 50%
NYC SCHE: owners 65+ with combined income up to $58,399
NYC deadline: March 15 for the tax year starting July 1
Outside NYC: file Form RP-467 with your assessor, usually by March 1
Separate from Enhanced STAR; getting one does not give you the other
body:
The senior citizens homeowners' exemption lowers property taxes for owners 65 and older with modest incomes by reducing the home's taxable assessment by up to 50%. It comes from Section 467 of the Real Property Tax Law. In New York City it is called SCHE (the Senior Citizen Homeowners' Exemption), and the income limit is $58,399.

Outside the city, each town, city, county and school district decides whether to offer it and at what income level. That means your mom in Rochester and your aunt in Islip might face different limits even though they are the same age with the same income. This guide covers both versions, the forms, the deadlines and the renewal rules that trip people up.

Who qualifies for the senior exemption outside New York City?

The Tax Department lists these rules for the statewide program:

  • Age. Generally 65 or older by the taxable status date, which is March 1 in most communities. Every owner must be 65 or older, unless the owners are spouses or siblings with a common parent, in which case one owner at 65 is enough. Some localities let owners who turn 65 after the taxable status date but by December 31 qualify. Ask your assessor.
  • Ownership. You must have owned the property for at least 12 consecutive months before filing. This is waived if you got the exemption on your previous home. Certain transfers, such as to a surviving spouse, do not break the 12 months.
  • Residency. The home must be the legal residence of all owners and used only as a residence. A partial exemption is possible if part of it is used for something else. There are exceptions for an owner in a residential health care facility, and for a spouse absent because of divorce, separation or abandonment.
  • Children in school. Generally, you are not eligible if a child living in the home attends public school. A child in private or parochial school does not count against you. School districts can choose to offer the exemption anyway.

How does the income scale work?

Each locality sets its own top income limit for the full 50% reduction, anywhere from $3,000 to $50,000. Localities that use the $50,000 limit can give more than 50% to lower incomes, and can add a sliding scale of smaller reductions for incomes just above the limit. The Tax Department lists these options. Your assessor has the exact local scale.

Income (if your locality uses the $50,000 limit)Exemption the locality can offer
Less than $47,00065%
$47,000 to less than $48,00060%
$48,000 to less than $49,00055%
$49,000 to less than $50,00050%
Sliding scale up to $55,70020%
Sliding scale up to $57,50010%
Sliding scale up to $58,4005%

Income starts with federal adjusted gross income, with some changes set by law. A spouse's income counts unless the spouse is absent because of legal separation or abandonment. Losses are capped at $3,000 per category and $15,000 in total. Which year counts depends on your community's taxable status date. If it falls before April 15, the assessor uses income from two years before. If it falls on or after April 15, the assessor uses the most recent calendar year.

How do I apply outside New York City?

You file with your local assessor. The forms are on the Tax Department's website.

  1. Find your assessor. Look up your town or city assessor in the state's Municipal Data Portal, or call town hall.
  2. Pick the right form. First-time applicants use Form RP-467. Renewals use RP-467-Rnw. If no one had to file a federal return, use the worksheet RP-467-Wkst. The instructions are in RP-467-I.
  3. Gather proof. First-time applicants need proof of age. Include a copy of the federal tax return if one was filed. The assessor may ask for more income records.
  4. File by the deadline. It is usually March 1, but dates vary, so confirm with your assessor. Some municipalities accept late filing for hardship or renewals.
  5. Bought after the deadline? You can apply within 30 days of the purchase. The assessor then has 30 days to decide.

Renewal timing depends on your locality, and the assessor can tell you how often your parent must file Form RP-467-Rnw. When a renewal form arrives, put a reminder on the calendar right away, because a missed renewal can mean a full tax bill the next year.

The senior exemption and Enhanced STAR are two different programs. Getting one does not sign you up for the other.

How does SCHE work in New York City?

In the five boroughs, the NYC Department of Finance runs the program as SCHE. The rules are close to the statewide ones, with the city's own income scale.

  • Age. All owners must be 65 or older. If the owners are spouses or siblings, only one needs to be 65.
  • Income. Combined income of the owners and spouses cannot be more than $58,399.
  • Ownership. At least 12 consecutive months before filing, waived if you had the exemption on your previous home.
  • Residency. All owners must live in the property as their primary residence, with exceptions for divorce, separation, abandonment, or an owner receiving inpatient care in a residential health care facility.
Combined income (NYC SCHE)Reduction in assessed value

$50,001 to $50,99945%
$51,000 to $51,99940%
$52,000 to $52,99935%
$53,000 to $53,89930%
$53,900 to $54,79925%
$54,800 to $55,69920%
$55,700 to $56,59915%
$56,600 to $57,49910%
$57,500 to $58,3995%

What counts as income for SCHE?

Finance uses adjusted gross income minus the taxable part of any IRA or individual retirement annuity distributions. If you do not file a tax return, income is based on what you would have reported. Owners who received SCHE before June 13, 2024 may use an older method. It counts Social Security, retirement benefits, interest, dividends, capital gains, net rental income, wages and self-employment income, and it lets you subtract unreimbursed medical and prescription drug costs. Finance offers an optional income worksheet to help you estimate.

Say your mom owns a condo in Flushing, files a joint return with your dad, and their adjusted gross income is $52,400 after subtracting the taxable part of his IRA withdrawals. On the city's scale, that lands in the $52,000 to $52,999 row, so the home's assessed value would drop by 35%.

How do I apply for SCHE, and when is the deadline?

Apply or renew by March 15 to receive the benefit in the tax year that begins July 1. If March 15 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

  1. Go online if you can. The online application on the Finance SCHE page is open September 28 to March 15. There is a separate version for co-op owners.
  2. Or use paper. Download the SCHE initial application and mail it. Forms come in Arabic, Bengali, Chinese, French, Haitian Creole, Korean, Polish, Russian, Spanish and Urdu.
  3. Work out income first. Use the Finance income worksheet and have tax returns or benefit statements for every owner and spouse at hand.
  4. Watch the mail. Finance sends a notice when it is time to renew. SCHE renewals are due every two years, also by March 15.

Questions go to 311. Finance also takes questions online through nyc.gov/contactdof. If a disability makes the paperwork hard, ask for an accommodation through 311 or the Finance Disability Service Facilitator.

What about the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption?

New York City also offers DHE (the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption) for owners with a disability. It uses the same $58,399 income limit and a reduction of up to 50% that shrinks to 5% at the top of the scale. Proof can be an award letter from the Social Security Administration, the Railroad Retirement Board or the U.S. Postal Service, a Commission for the Blind certificate, a Workers' Compensation Board award order, or a VA letter confirming a disability pension. DHE must be renewed every year by March 15. You cannot receive both SCHE and DHE. If you qualify for both, you get SCHE.

Outside the city, if some owners qualify for the senior exemption and others for the disability exemption, the owners can choose whichever helps more.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Skipping STAR. The senior exemption and STAR are separate programs. A parent who has neither needs to register for STAR and apply for the senior exemption. Our STAR guide explains how.
  • Missing a renewal. In the city, SCHE renews every two years and DHE every year. Outside the city, follow your assessor's schedule.
  • Counting IRA withdrawals. The city subtracts the taxable IRA amount from adjusted gross income. Check before deciding a parent earns too much.
  • Not asking about a move to care. If your parent moves into a nursing home or other residential health care facility, ask the assessor or Finance how the residency exception applies before assuming the exemption ends.
  • Paying a stranger to file. These applications are free. If someone offers to get a parent's taxes lowered for a fee, call the assessor or 311 first.
Renting instead of owning?

New York City renters 62 and older may be able to freeze their rent through SCRIE. See our guide to SCRIE and DRIE.

faq.q: What is the income limit for SCHE in NYC?
faq.a: Combined income of all owners and spouses cannot be more than $58,399. Income up to $50,000 gets the full 50% reduction, and the reduction shrinks in steps down to 5% between $57,500 and $58,399.

faq.q: How do I get my mom the senior property tax exemption in Staten Island?
faq.a: Apply for SCHE with the NYC Department of Finance online or on paper between September 28 and March 15. All owners must be 65 or older (one is enough for spouses or siblings) and she must have owned the home for 12 months.

faq.q: Where does my dad in Albany County file for the senior citizens exemption?
faq.a: He files Form RP-467 with his town or city assessor, usually by March 1. Ask the assessor what income limit the town, county and school district use, since each sets its own.

faq.q: How often do I renew SCHE?
faq.a: Every two years. Finance sends a notice when renewal is due, and the renewal must be filed by March 15. DHE must be renewed every year.

faq.q: Does the senior exemption include Enhanced STAR?
faq.a: No. They are separate programs. A parent who already gets Basic STAR is upgraded to Enhanced STAR automatically when eligible, but the senior exemption is its own application, filed with the assessor or, in New York City, with Finance as SCHE.

faq.q: Can I get both SCHE and the Disabled Homeowners' Exemption?
faq.a: No. In New York City you cannot receive both. If you qualify for both, Finance gives you SCHE.

title: SNAP for New Yorkers 60 and older: income limits and how to apply
seoTitle: SNAP for NY Seniors 60+: Income Limits 2026 to 2027
seoDesc: SNAP income limits for New Yorkers 60+ from October 2026, the medical deduction, SSI auto-enrollment, how to apply in NYC or upstate, and market coupons.
dek: A New Yorker 60 or older living alone can have gross income up to $2,660 a month and still qualify for SNAP. Here are the current limits, the rules that help older adults, and how to apply in New York City and the rest of the state.
keyFacts: Gross income limit for one person with a member 60+: $2,660 a month
Maximum benefit: $306 for one person, $562 for two
Figures run October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027
Out-of-pocket medical costs over $35 a month can be deducted
State SNAP hotline: 1-800-342-3009
body:
Yes, many older New Yorkers qualify for SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, once called food stamps). If anyone in the household is 60 or older or disabled, New York lets a one-person household have gross income up to $2,660 a month and still be screened in. These limits took effect on October 1, 2026 and run through September 30, 2027.

The maximum benefit is $306 a month for one person and $562 for two. Most people get less, because SNAP counts part of your own income toward food. Still, plenty of retirees on Social Security get a real monthly amount, and older adults get extra deductions that younger people do not. This guide covers the limits, the special rules, the automatic program for people on SSI, how to apply in New York City and upstate, and the farmers market coupons for people 60 and older.

Who qualifies for SNAP at 60 or older?

New York uses three income charts. The one that matters here covers households with a member 60 or older or a disabled member. It is set at 200% of the federal poverty line. Gross income means income before anything is taken out, so use the Social Security amount before the Medicare premium is deducted.

Household sizeMonthly gross incomeYearly gross income
1$2,660$31,920
2$3,607$43,280
3$4,553$54,640
4$5,500$66,000
Each extra personadd $947add $11,360

Under this chart, most households do not face a savings test. The state says assets such as savings, stocks and retirement accounts are not counted for most households. That surprises many families who assume a parent with a little money in the bank cannot apply.

What if income is above the chart?

An older household above 200% is not automatically out. Federal rules say a household with a member 60 or older or disabled only has to pass the net income test. Net income is what is left after deductions. For October 2026 to September 2027, the net limit is $1,330 a month for one person and $1,804 for two. In that case a resource limit also applies, which is $4,750 for households with a member 60 or older or disabled.

Who counts as disabled?

For SNAP, a person counts as disabled if they get SSI, Social Security disability or blindness benefits, a government disability retirement for a permanent disability, or certain VA benefits. The full list is on the USDA page in the sources below.

A parent with savings in the bank can still get SNAP. Most New York households face no asset test.

How much SNAP could my parent get?

The benefit depends on household size, income and allowed costs. Here are the most a household can receive each month through September 2027.

Household sizeMaximum monthly benefit
1$306
2$562
3$808
4$1,023

Eligible households of one or two people get at least $25 a month. The office subtracts a standard deduction from income first ($217 a month for households of one to three people). Then it looks at housing costs. Rent or mortgage, property taxes, homeowner's insurance and utilities can all lower countable income.

Older households get two breaks here. First, most households have their shelter deduction capped at $769 a month, but households with a member 60 or older or disabled have no cap. Second, they can deduct medical costs, which is the next section. Both rules only help if you report the costs, so bring the bills.

What medical costs can older adults deduct?

If you are 60 or older or disabled, verified out-of-pocket medical costs over $35 a month can be deducted from countable income. Only the part above $35 counts. A lower countable income means a higher benefit. The state's guide for older adults lists costs that can count, including:

  • Health insurance premiums and deductibles, including the Medicare Part B premium if you pay it yourself.
  • Doctor, dental, hospital and therapy bills not paid by insurance, Medicare or Medicaid.
  • Prescription drugs and delivery, plus over-the-counter medicine approved by a provider.
  • Hearing aids, eyeglasses, dentures, adult diapers and similar supplies.
  • Wheelchairs, prosthetics and personal emergency response systems.
  • Rides to medical appointments or the pharmacy, including bus, subway or taxi fare and mileage in your own car.
  • Home health care or adult day care related to age or disability.

Say your dad lives alone in Utica and pays $90 a month for a Medigap plan plus $60 for prescriptions. That is $150 a month. He can deduct the $115 above the $35 floor. Once his costs are verified, they do not have to be proven again unless they change. Report one-time costs too, such as new glasses.

If he pays the Medicare Part B premium himself, note that it is $209.40 a month in 2027. If he could use help with that premium, read our guide to the Medicare Savings Program.

What if my parent gets SSI?

New York has an automatic program for many people on SSI (Supplemental Security Income). It is called NYSCAP, the New York State Combined Application Project. It replaced the older NYSNIP program. Existing NYSNIP cases were switched over by November 30, 2024. If you have heard of NYSNIP, this is the program that took its place.

NYSCAP covers single SSI recipients whom Social Security codes as living alone. Social Security's idea of living alone can include some people who share a home. Eligible people are enrolled without filing a SNAP application. The case opens with a basic budget using SSI and other income, with only the standard deduction.

That first amount can be low. The fix is to report rent, utilities and medical costs to the local social services office. The office then recalculates using regular SNAP rules, which can raise the benefit. There is no option to opt out of NYSCAP if you are eligible, and cases are certified for 36 months.

Is there an easier form for other older households?

Yes. New York has a simplified application project for households where every adult is 60 or older or disabled and nobody has earnings from work. These households can be certified for up to 36 months and usually do not need an interview to recertify. The short form is the LDSS-5166. Proof of residency and medical costs is still required.

Receiving SNAP does not reduce SSI or Social Security disability payments, according to NYC HRA. For the SSI and state supplement amounts, see our Social Security 2027 guide.

How do I apply in New York City?

In the five boroughs, SNAP runs through the Human Resources Administration (HRA). The easiest way to apply is online with ACCESS HRA. You can also apply in person, by mail, or through an authorized representative, such as an adult child.

  • Interview. Everyone must complete an interview after applying. HRA will not call you to set it up, so you call them. The DSS OneNumber is 718-557-1399 (press 2 for SNAP).
  • Documents. Upload copies with ACCESS HRA Mobile, fax them to 917-639-2544, or bring them to a SNAP Center. Send copies and keep the originals.
  • Timing. HRA must decide within 30 days. A household with little or no income or resources may get expedited SNAP within 7 days.
  • SSI households. If everyone in the household gets SSI or is applying for it, HRA says you may apply at a Social Security office.

How do I apply outside New York City?

Everywhere else, SNAP runs through your county Department of Social Services. You can apply online at myBenefits.ny.gov, or contact your county office to apply there. The state SNAP hotline is 1-800-342-3009, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Each county runs its own office. In Erie County, for example, you can apply in person on the 3rd floor of the Rath Building, 158 Pearl Street, Buffalo. The Erie County SNAP call center is 716-858-7239. Find your own county office on our county pages or through the state hotline.

If every adult in the household is 60 or older or disabled and getting to the office is hard, ask for a phone interview. State rules let these households have the office interview waived and done by phone or a home visit.

  1. Gather papers. Social Security award letter or SSA-1099, pension statements, rent or mortgage statement, property tax bill, homeowner's insurance bill, utility bills and medical bills.
  2. Pick the right door. ACCESS HRA in the five boroughs. myBenefits.ny.gov or the county Department of Social Services everywhere else.
  3. Name a helper if needed. An adult child can be the authorized representative. The designation must be in writing and signed.
  4. Do the interview. In NYC, call to complete it. Upstate and on Long Island, ask for a phone interview if travel is hard.
  5. Report costs. List every medical and housing cost. These are what raise an older adult's benefit.
  6. Watch the mail. Answer any request for documents quickly, and keep copies of everything you send.

What are the senior farmers market coupons?

The Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program gives low-income New Yorkers 60 and older a booklet of coupons for fresh local fruits and vegetables. Each booklet is worth $25, made up of five $5 coupons. The program starts July 1 each year, and booklets go out first come, first served.

  • Outside New York City. Booklets come through your county Office for the Aging. The state line for details is 800-342-9871.
  • In New York City. NYC Aging handed out 2026 booklets from July through September 30, and coupons had to be spent by November 30, 2026. The 2026 income limit was $2,461 a month for one person. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 about next season.

SNAP itself also works at many farmers markets and farm stands. At participating markets, for every $2 in SNAP you swap for wooden tokens, the manager may add a $2 FreshConnect Check. Look for the FreshConnect sign.

What mistakes cost older adults benefits?

  • Not applying because of savings. Most New York households face no asset test.
  • Skipping medical bills. Without them, an older adult misses the deduction that matters most.
  • Leaving out housing costs on an SSI case. NYSCAP opens with only the standard deduction. Report rent and utilities to raise it.
  • Missing the interview. In NYC you have to call. A missed interview can mean a denial.
  • Not checking other help. SNAP households often also qualify for HEAP heating help, EPIC drug coverage or Extra Help with Part D.

The only way to know for sure is to apply. If you are unsure, the state hotline at 1-800-342-3009 can answer questions before you file.

faq.q: How do I help my mom apply for SNAP in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Apply online through ACCESS HRA at nyc.gov/accesshra, or in person or by mail. You can act as her authorized representative. After applying, call the DSS OneNumber at 718-557-1399 (press 2) to do the interview, because HRA will not call to schedule it.

faq.q: Can my dad in Rochester get SNAP if he has savings?
faq.a: Probably yes. If his household's gross income is under New York's chart for older adults ($2,660 a month for one person through September 2027), most households face no savings test. Apply through myBenefits.ny.gov or the Monroe County Department of Social Services.

faq.q: What is the SNAP income limit for a senior living alone in New York?
faq.a: For October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027, a one-person household with a member 60 or older can have gross income up to $2,660 a month ($31,920 a year). Above that, the household may still qualify by passing the net income test of $1,330 a month.

faq.q: What happened to NYSNIP?
faq.a: NYSNIP was phased out in 2024, with cases switched over by November 30, 2024. It was replaced by NYSCAP, which automatically enrolls single SSI recipients that Social Security codes as living alone. Report rent, utility and medical costs to your local office so the benefit is recalculated under regular SNAP rules.

faq.q: Can seniors deduct medical expenses for SNAP in New York?
faq.a: Yes. If you are 60 or older or disabled, verified out-of-pocket medical costs above $35 a month can be deducted, which raises the benefit. Premiums, prescriptions, dental bills, hearing aids and rides to medical visits can count.

faq.q: How do older adults get farmers market coupons in New York?
faq.a: Low-income New Yorkers 60 and older can get a $25 coupon booklet each season starting July 1. Outside NYC, contact your county Office for the Aging or call 800-342-9871. In NYC, call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.

title: Social Security in 2027: what changes for New Yorkers
seoTitle: Social Security 2027 in New York: COLA, SSI and SSP
seoDesc: The 2027 Social Security raise is 3.6%. See the new average check, earnings limits, SSI and New York State Supplement amounts, Medicare costs and SSA contacts.
dek: Social Security and SSI checks rise 3.6% for 2027. Here is what that means for the average retiree, the new work limits, SSI and the New York State Supplement, the Medicare premium that comes out first, and how to reach a Social Security office in New York.
keyFacts: 2027 cost-of-living raise: 3.6%
Average retired worker: $2,095 before, $2,170 after the raise
SSI federal rate 2027: $1,029 single, $1,544 couple
Medicare Part B premium 2027: $209.40 a month
body:
Social Security and SSI payments go up 3.6% for 2027. Social Security checks rise starting with benefits payable in January 2027, and SSI payments rise starting December 31, 2026.

For the average retired worker, that means a monthly check of about $2,170, up from $2,095. Most people will see less than the full raise in the bank, because the Medicare Part B premium also goes up, to $209.40 a month. This guide walks through the new numbers, the rules for working while collecting, SSI and the New York State Supplement, and how to reach Social Security in New York.

How much is the 2027 raise?

The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is 3.6%. It was announced in October 2026. Here is what the Social Security Administration (SSA) says it does to average checks.

Average monthly benefitBefore the raiseAfter the raise (January 2027)
All retired workers$2,095$2,170
Aged couple, both receiving benefits$3,238$3,355

The largest benefit for a worker who retires at full retirement age in 2027 is $4,188 a month, up from $4,152 in 2026. For people still working, the most earnings taxed for Social Security rises to $192,300, from $184,500. It takes $1,970 in earnings to earn one work credit in 2027, up from $1,890.

Example: a widow in Syracuse

Say your mom gets $1,900 a month from Social Security before Medicare is taken out. A 3.6% raise adds about $68, bringing her to roughly $1,968. Her Part B premium rises $6.50, from $202.90 to $209.40. So her deposit grows by about $62. Her exact new amount will be in her COLA notice.

When will my parent find out the new amount?

Social Security sends a COLA notice. Most people who had a my Social Security account at ssa.gov by November 18, 2026 can read it online in the Message Center starting in late November. The notice shows the new benefit and what will be taken out for Medicare in 2027. You can also choose to get notices online instead of by mail.

If you help a parent, setting up their account together lets you both read Social Security notices as soon as they post, without waiting for the mail.

How much can I earn while collecting in 2027?

If you collect Social Security before your full retirement age and keep working, Social Security holds back $1 in benefits for every $2 you earn above a yearly limit. In the year you reach full retirement age, it holds back $1 for every $3 above a higher limit. Once you reach full retirement age, earnings no longer reduce benefits, and Social Security recalculates your check to credit back what was held.

Earnings test limit20262027
Under full retirement age all year$24,480 a year ($2,040 a month)$25,560 a year ($2,130 a month)
Year you reach full retirement age$65,160 a year ($5,430 a month)$67,920 a year ($5,660 a month)

In the year you reach full retirement age, only earnings up to the month before you reach it count. Report expected earnings to Social Security if you plan to work, so your checks are not overpaid and later clawed back.

Example: working part time in Westchester

Say you are 63, collecting Social Security, and earn $35,560 from a part-time job in 2027. That is $10,000 over the $25,560 limit. Social Security would hold back $1 for every $2 over, or $5,000 for the year. Once you reach full retirement age, your monthly benefit is recalculated to credit those months back.

Benefits held back under the earnings test are credited back once you reach full retirement age.

What are the SSI and New York State Supplement amounts?

SSI (Supplemental Security Income) is a monthly payment for people 65 or older, blind or disabled who have little income and few resources. The federal rate for 2027 is $1,029 a month for one person and $1,544 for a couple, up from $994 and $1,491 in 2026.

New York adds its own payment on top, called the State Supplement Program (SSP). It is run by the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA). The amount depends on where and how you live. These are the 2026 state amounts, the latest chart OTDA has posted.

Living arrangement (2026)NY State Supplement, individualNY State Supplement, couple
Living alone$87$104
Living with others$23$46
Family Care (NYC, Nassau, Rockland, Suffolk, Westchester)$266.48$1,029.96
Residential Care (NYC, Nassau, Rockland, Suffolk, Westchester)$435$1,367
Residential Care (rest of state)$405$1,307
Enhanced Residential Care$694$1,885

In 2026, a person living alone got $994 from SSI plus $87 from New York, for a total of $1,081. A couple living alone got $1,595. Check OTDA's maximum benefit chart for the 2027 totals once it is posted.

Who qualifies for SSI in New York?

  • Age 65 or older, or blind or disabled.
  • A New York resident who meets citizenship or qualified immigrant rules.
  • Countable resources of $2,000 or less for one person, or $3,000 for a couple.
  • Limited income from all sources, including Social Security.

The SSI raise begins with the payment dated December 31, 2026. OTDA's schedule for the state supplement shows the same pattern, with January benefits paid on December 31. That deposit is the January payment arriving early, so plan the month around it.

There is no online SSI application. You apply by setting up an appointment with Social Security. Questions about the state payment go to the SSP Customer Service line at 1-855-488-0541, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

Many SSI recipients who live alone are enrolled in SNAP automatically. See our SNAP guide for how that works and how to raise the amount.

How does Medicare affect the 2027 check?

If Medicare Part B comes out of your Social Security, the 2027 standard premium is $209.40 a month. That is $6.50 more than the 2026 premium of $202.90. The Part B deductible for 2027 is $292.

A federal hold-harmless rule protects most people whose premium is deducted from their check. If the COLA is too small to cover the premium increase, your net benefit cannot go down. This protection does not apply to people who pay the higher income-related premium. For the full list of 2027 Medicare costs, see our Medicare costs 2027 guide.

If money is tight, two programs can take the Part B premium off your bill or lower drug costs. Read about the Medicare Savings Program and Extra Help. New York does not tax Social Security, which our retirement tax guide explains.

How do I reach a Social Security office in New York?

The national number is 1-800-772-1213. Deaf or hard of hearing callers can use TTY 1-800-325-0778.

  1. Try the phone first. Social Security lists many services you can handle through the national number, which can save a trip.
  2. Find the right office. Enter a ZIP code in the Social Security office locator to get the address, phone number and hours of the office that serves that area.
  3. Call ahead. Call the local office or the national number to book an appointment instead of walking in.
  4. Know about card centers. In Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan, original and replacement Social Security cards are handled at Social Security Card Centers, listed on SSA's New York page.
  5. Bring papers. Photo ID, your Social Security number, and any letter you are asking about.
  6. Bring a helper if needed. An adult child can come along. For ongoing help managing benefits, ask Social Security about naming a representative payee.

How can I help a parent who has not claimed yet?

If your mom or dad is still deciding when to start benefits, a few steps make the choice clearer. None of them cost anything.

  • Open a my Social Security account together. It shows notices online and lets you check the record Social Security has on file.
  • Look at the work record. Missing years of earnings can lower a benefit. Ask Social Security how to correct them while the paperwork still exists.
  • Think about work plans. If they will keep working before full retirement age, the earnings test above may hold back part of the check for now.
  • Line up Medicare. Medicare and Social Security are separate decisions. Our Medicare enrollment guide covers the dates.
  • Book the appointment early. Use the locator or the national number, and write down the name of anyone you speak with.

What should families watch out for?

  • Scam calls. Social Security warns that scammers threaten to suspend your number and insist on payment by gift card, wire transfer or cash. Hang up, then report it to the Inspector General at oig.ssa.gov/report.
  • Unreported work. Earnings above the limit that are not reported can lead to an overpayment notice later.
  • Missing the COLA notice. It shows the Medicare deduction and the new amount. Save it with your tax papers.
  • Not checking other help. A parent on a small check may qualify for SSI, SNAP, HEAP or EPIC.

faq.q: How much will my mom's Social Security go up in January 2027?
faq.a: Benefits rise 3.6%. On a $1,900 check that is about $68 more before Medicare. Her exact amount, and what Medicare takes out, will be in her COLA notice, available online in her my Social Security account.

faq.q: Where is the Social Security office for my dad in Staten Island?
faq.a: Enter his ZIP code in SSA's office locator at ssa.gov/locator to get the address, phone and hours of the office that serves him. You can also call 1-800-772-1213 to set up an appointment.

faq.q: What is the 2027 SSI amount in New York?
faq.a: The federal SSI rate for 2027 is $1,029 a month for one person and $1,544 for a couple. New York adds a State Supplement. In 2026 that was $87 a month for a person living alone and $104 for a couple living alone.

faq.q: How much can I earn in 2027 and still collect Social Security?
faq.a: If you are under full retirement age all year, the 2027 limit is $25,560. In the year you reach full retirement age, it is $67,920, counting only earnings before the month you reach it. After that, earnings no longer reduce benefits.

faq.q: What is the Medicare Part B premium in 2027?
faq.a: The standard Part B premium for 2027 is $209.40 a month, up $6.50 from $202.90. The Part B deductible is $292.

faq.q: When do SSI payments go up?
faq.a: The 3.6% raise for SSI starts with the payment on December 31, 2026. Social Security retirement and disability checks go up starting with benefits payable in January 2027.

title: Basic and Enhanced STAR in New York: limits, rules and how to apply
seoTitle: Enhanced STAR NY: 2026 and 2027 Income Limits
seoDesc: Enhanced STAR in New York: the $110,750 and $113,550 income limits, credit vs exemption, the Income Verification Program and how to register by phone or online.
dek: STAR cuts school taxes for New York homeowners, and the Enhanced version gives more to owners 65 and older. Here is who qualifies, what changed with the credit, and how to sign up.
keyFacts: Enhanced STAR income limit: $110,750 for 2026, $113,550 for 2027
At least one resident owner must be 65 by December 31
New homeowners can only get the STAR credit, paid by check or direct deposit
Since 2026, the state upgrades eligible owners to Enhanced STAR automatically
STAR help line: 518-457-2036, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
body:
STAR (the School Tax Relief program) lowers the school tax cost for New York homeowners who live in the home. Enhanced STAR is the bigger version for owners 65 and older, and the income limit is $110,750 for 2026 benefits and $113,550 for 2027 benefits.

There are two ways STAR reaches you. Most people who bought a home in recent years get the STAR credit, a check or direct deposit from the state Department of Taxation and Finance. Some longtime owners still get the older STAR exemption, which shows up as a reduction on the school tax bill. The rules for getting Enhanced STAR depend on which one your household has. This guide walks through both, so you or your mom or dad can see exactly what to do next.

What is the difference between the STAR credit and the STAR exemption?

The STAR exemption reduces your school tax bill directly. It is closed to new homeowners. If you have received it since 2015 for the same primary residence, you can keep it. The law does not let the exemption move with you to a new home. If the seller of a home had the exemption, the buyer may keep it for the first year only, then must register for the credit.

The STAR credit is a payment sent to you by check or direct deposit. The Tax Department says to expect it around the time you receive your school tax bill. The state says the credit may increase by as much as 2% each year, while the exemption cannot increase and cannot be larger than the credit would be.

STAR creditSTAR exemption
How you get itCheck or direct deposit from the stateReduction on your school tax bill
Open to new homeowners?YesNo (only owners who have had it since 2015 for the same home)
Basic STAR income limit$500,000$250,000
Enhanced STAR income limit$110,750 for 2026 benefits; $113,550 for 2027 benefits
Can it grow?May rise up to 2% a yearCannot increase
Where to apply for EnhancedAutomatic upgrade by the Tax DepartmentAutomatic upgrade since 2026 (the state tells your assessor)

You can switch from the exemption to the credit in the state's Homeowner Benefit Portal. Once you switch, you cannot switch back. If you switch before your community's deadline, the first credit comes that same year. If you switch after the deadline but by December 31, you keep the exemption on that year's bill and the credit starts the next year.

Since 2026, turning 65 should bring the Enhanced amount without a new application, for credit and exemption holders alike.

Who qualifies for Enhanced STAR?

The Tax Department lists these rules for Enhanced STAR:

  • Age. At least one resident owner must be 65 or older as of December 31 of the year the benefit is for. It does not matter how the owners are related.
  • Income. Combined income must be $110,750 or less for 2026 benefits and $113,550 or less for 2027 benefits. Only the income of owners and their spouses who live at the property counts.
  • Which income. The state uses federal adjusted gross income minus the taxable amount of IRA distributions. It looks back two years. For 2026 benefits, it uses the 2024 tax year.
  • Ownership. You must own the home as of July 1 of the benefit year. Buyers under a land contract count as owners. Homes held by a corporation, partnership or LLC do not qualify unless it is a farm dwelling.
  • Primary residence. The home must be your main residence as of July 1. The state looks at where you spend your time, where you vote, and the address on your car registration and ID.
  • One benefit per couple. A married couple can receive only one STAR benefit, no matter how many homes they own, unless they are legally separated.

The state describes the Enhanced benefit as based on the first $91,700 of a home's full value for the 2027 to 2028 school year. Basic STAR is based on the first $30,000. What that means in dollars depends on your school district's tax rate, so two neighbors in different districts can see very different amounts.

Say your dad turns 65 in August 2027, owns a house in Schenectady County with his wife, and their combined 2025 adjusted gross income was $64,000 with no taxable IRA withdrawals. He meets the age test for 2027 (65 by December 31), and the couple is under the $113,550 limit. Whether they get the credit or the exemption, the state says it upgrades eligible owners on its own in the year a resident owner turns 65.

How do I register for the STAR credit?

If your parent bought the home recently, or never signed up, the path is the STAR credit. The Tax Department says new homeowners should register as soon as the home becomes their primary residence. You register online, or by calling the STAR line at 518-457-2036 (weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.).

  1. Open an online account. Log in to or create an Individual Online Services account with the Tax Department.
  2. Find the portal. Choose the Services menu, then Real property tax, then Homeowner Benefit Portal, then Register.
  3. Have the details ready. You need the names and Social Security numbers of all owners and their spouses, the school district, the approximate purchase date, and the tax returns for the income year the state uses (2024 returns for the 2026 credit).
  4. Answer every question carefully. If an owner did not have to file a tax return, the portal asks for the income details instead.
  5. Save the confirmation number. Write it down or print it. You will want it if you call later.
  6. Sign up for direct deposit. In the same portal, enroll in STAR Credit Direct Deposit. Do it early. If you enroll fewer than 15 days before the payment is issued, you get a paper check that year.

Missed a year? The state lets you register up to three years after the income tax filing deadline for the year in question. To be eligible for interest on a late credit, you must register on or before July 1 of the credit year.

Update the registration when ownership changes because of marriage, divorce, survivorship after a co-owner dies, a trust or a name change. Close it if you sell the home. The Property Tax Credit Lookup shows what the state has sent you.

How does a senior with the STAR exemption get Enhanced STAR?

The rules changed in 2026. The Tax Department says owners who still get the exemption on their school tax bill no longer need to apply with the local assessor for Enhanced STAR when they turn 65. The state notifies the assessor and upgrades the home automatically, as long as the owners are otherwise eligible. If a resident owner was already 65, the upgrade was set to begin with 2026 benefits.

If your parent turned 65 and the school tax bill still shows only Basic STAR, call the assessor first, then the STAR line. Owners who apply through the assessor have used Form RP-425-E with Form RP-425-IVP, and the assessor checks age and income in the first year.

What is the Income Verification Program?

The Income Verification Program (IVP) lets the state check your income every year so you do not have to. All Enhanced STAR exemption recipients must take part. In the first year, the assessor checks your eligibility from the papers you provide. After that, the state verifies your income on its own. You do not reapply or hand the assessor copies of your returns. The assessor is told only if you meet the limit. Your actual income stays private.

What are the assessor deadlines?

The state's Income Verification Program page lists these local filing deadlines for owners who file with the assessor.

Where you liveDeadline to file with the assessor
Most communitiesMarch 1
Towns in Westchester CountyMay 1 or June 1
Nassau CountyJanuary 2 (Form RP-425-IVP goes with the county's Enhanced STAR application)
Villages of Bronxville and Kiryas JoelJanuary 1
CitiesCheck with your assessor

If your parent missed the deadline for a good reason, there is a late option. Senior citizens can ask the Commissioner of Taxation and Finance for permission to file a late Enhanced STAR application. The request is due by the last day to pay school taxes without interest or penalty, and you must show good cause for missing the taxable status date. The Tax Department checks with the assessor and then tells both of you its decision.

If your parent moves or the home stops being the primary residence, tell the assessor.

How does STAR work in New York City?

The NYC Department of Finance says it no longer administers STAR or Enhanced STAR and does not accept STAR applications. Homeowners in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island register for the STAR credit with the state through the Homeowner Benefit Portal or by calling 518-457-2036. Existing recipients in the city also contact the state to report an ownership change or an upgrade from Basic to Enhanced STAR.

New York City has its own senior property tax break, the Senior Citizen Homeowners' Exemption (SCHE), which Finance does run. It is a separate program with a separate application. See our guide to the senior citizens homeowners' exemption.

What mistakes cost seniors their STAR benefit?

  • Assuming the senior exemption covers STAR. The state says the senior citizens exemption and Enhanced STAR are separate. Getting one does not give you the other.
  • Switching without comparing. Switching to the credit can be worth more in some communities, and the state publishes examples. Because you cannot switch back, compare first, then decide.
  • Forgetting the IRA rule. The taxable part of IRA distributions is subtracted from income for STAR. Families sometimes count those withdrawals and wrongly assume a parent is over the limit.
  • Not updating after a death. When a spouse dies, the surviving owner should update the registration so the benefit continues in the right name.
  • Answering calls or texts that ask for STAR fees. Registering is free. If someone calls asking for a payment to keep your STAR, hang up and call the official number yourself.
Other tax help for homeowners 65 and older

STAR is only one piece. Many towns, cities and counties also offer the senior citizens exemption. See our guides to the senior exemption and retirement income tax in New York.

Where can I get help with STAR?

Call the Tax Department's STAR line at 518-457-2036, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For exemption questions, call your town or city assessor. Town or city hall can connect you, and your county Office for the Aging may be able to help a parent with the paperwork.

The state's STAR resource center has the credit delivery schedule for your area, handouts for new homeowners and answers to common questions.

faq.q: What is the Enhanced STAR income limit for 2027?
faq.a: The limit is $113,550 for 2027 benefits and $110,750 for 2026 benefits. The state uses federal adjusted gross income minus the taxable part of IRA distributions, for owners and resident spouses only.

faq.q: Does my mom in Buffalo need to apply for Enhanced STAR when she turns 65?
faq.a: In most cases, no. Since 2026 the Tax Department upgrades eligible owners to Enhanced STAR automatically in the year a resident owner turns 65, whether she gets the STAR credit or the exemption. If her check or school tax bill does not change, call her assessor or 518-457-2036.

faq.q: How do I sign up my dad in Brooklyn for STAR?
faq.a: NYC Finance no longer handles STAR. Register him for the STAR credit with the state through the Homeowner Benefit Portal in an Individual Online Services account, or call 518-457-2036.

faq.q: Do both owners have to be 65 for Enhanced STAR?
faq.a: No. The Tax Department says only one resident owner must be at least 65 as of December 31 of the benefit year, however the owners are related.

faq.q: Can I switch back to the STAR exemption after taking the credit?
faq.a: No. Once you switch to the STAR credit, you cannot switch back to the exemption.

faq.q: What is the STAR phone number?
faq.a: The Tax Department's STAR line is 518-457-2036, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
