title: Utility help and shutoff protections for older New Yorkers
seoTitle: NY Utility Shutoff Protections and Bill Help for Seniors
seoDesc: New York rules that protect customers 62+ from gas and electric shutoffs, medical and life-support certificates, HEAP, EAP discounts, Lifeline and PSC help.
dek: New York law gives older, blind and disabled utility customers extra protection from gas and electric shutoffs, with more from November 1 to April 15. Here is how those rules work, how to register medical equipment, and where to get help with the bill.
keyFacts: Households where every adult is 62+, blind or disabled get extra shutoff protections
A doctor's medical emergency certificate keeps service on for 30 days
Cold weather rules run November 1 to April 15
Utilities cannot require a deposit from customers 62+ in most cases
PSC shutoff hotline: 800-342-3355, weekdays 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.
body:
New York's Home Energy Fair Practices Act (HEFPA) gives gas, electric and steam customers a set of rights, and it adds extra protection for households where everyone is 62 or older, blind or disabled. A utility must try hard to reach those customers before any shutoff, and it must hold off while it brings in the local Department of Social Services. A doctor can also stop a shutoff for 30 days in a medical emergency, and for someone on life-support equipment, the doctor's certificate stays in effect unless the Public Service Commission ends it.

None of this means free power. The bill is still owed. But the rules give your mom or dad time to set up a payment plan or get help from the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP). This guide explains the protections, how to register, where to get money for the bill, and who to call when the utility will not listen.

What protections do customers 62 and older get?

If the utility knows that you and every adult living with you are 62 or older, blind or disabled, it must make special efforts before a shutoff. The New York State Department of Public Service (DPS) says the utility will try to reach you by phone or in person at least three days before the date. It will try to work out a payment agreement or get payment from Social Services or a private group. If nothing works, it tells Social Services and keeps the service on for another 15 business days.

If service is shut off anyway, the utility must try to reach you within 10 days after to see if service can be restored. The key step is telling the utility. DPS says to notify it right away so it can code the account. That information is kept confidential.

RuleWhat it means for an older customer
Notice before shutoffA Final Termination Notice, then at least 15 days to pay or make a plan
Contact before shutoff (62+, blind or disabled)Phone or in-person attempt at least 3 days before
If no arrangementSocial Services is notified and service continues 15 more business days
When shutoffs can happenOnly 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Thursday
No shutoffs onPublic holidays, the day before a holiday, the two weeks that include Christmas and New Year's Day
DepositsCannot be required from a customer 62 or older unless service was shut off for nonpayment in the past six months

Each utility applies the rule in its own words. National Grid, for example, says everyone in the home must be 62 or older, blind, or getting Social Security Disability, SSI or military benefits for a service-related disability, and anyone else in the home must be 18 or younger. It may ask you to recertify each year. Con Edison runs a free, confidential Senior Direct line for these households at 1-800-404-9097, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Tell the utility your parent is 62 or older now, before there is ever a past-due bill.

What changes from November 1 to April 15?

During the cold weather period, the rules cover every household, at any age. For heat-related service, the utility must try to reach you or another adult at home at least three days before a shutoff, and again on the day itself. It is checking whether losing heat could seriously harm anyone in the home.

If harm might result, the utility must tell Social Services, which investigates, and the utility cannot shut off for another 15 business days. If the utility could not reach an adult before shutting off, it must try to find out whether anyone lives there and could be harmed. If so, it restores service for 15 business days and calls Social Services. Tenants whose landlord stopped paying get at least 30 days' notice in this period when the service is heat related.

Is there protection in a heat wave?

Yes. On March 19, 2026, the Public Service Commission (PSC) approved extreme heat rules for the state's largest investor-owned electric and water utilities. They cannot shut off a home's service for nonpayment on any day the heat index is forecast to reach, or reaches, 90 degrees. In designated heat islands, the pause also covers the two days after. DPS says these protections apply any time of year when the heat conditions are met. The PSC only asked the Long Island Power Authority to consider the same protections for PSEG Long Island customers, so check with PSEG Long Island.

How does a medical emergency certificate work?

When a doctor or the local Board of Health tells the utility that a medical emergency would get worse without service, the utility must keep service on for 30 days. The doctor can call first, but a written certificate must follow within five business days. It can be renewed for another 30 days if the doctor explains why losing service would make the emergency worse and you show why you cannot pay the bill. A longer period can be approved for a chronic condition.

Your parent still has to make a reasonable effort to pay during this time. DPS staff can help set up a payment plan so a big balance does not pile up. Think of this certificate as breathing room after a hospital stay or a new diagnosis, while you apply for HEAP and other help.

How do I register my dad's oxygen concentrator or other life-support equipment?

Register it with the utility as soon as it comes home. Under HEFPA, when service is needed to run a life-support system, the doctor's certificate stays in effect unless the PSC ends it. Every three months, though, you must show the utility why the bill cannot be paid.

Registration also matters during outages. National Grid, for example, says it calls registered customers before planned outages and checks on them during long unplanned ones. National Grid and PSEG Long Island both say registering does not protect service from interruption, so you still need a backup plan, such as batteries, a generator or a place to go.

UtilityHow to register (as each utility states)
Con EdisonLife-support form in My Account, by mail or email, or call 1-877-582-6633. A doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or board of health official must certify within 30 days.
Orange & RocklandCall Customer Assistance at 1-877-434-4100, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. weekdays. A form signed by your health care provider is required. O&R says nebulizers and adult apnea monitors do not qualify.
Central HudsonLife Support Equipment Program application with a physician's certification, recertified every year. Central Hudson tags the meter and gives a confidential hotline number.
PSEG Long IslandCritical Care Program. Provide a medical certificate from a doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or local Board of Health, and call 1-800-490-0025. PSEG Long Island says joining does not guarantee priority restoration.
National Grid (upstate)Apply online, by email, fax or mail. National Grid sends a Physician Protection Form to the medical professional, puts a tag seal on the meter and requires yearly recertification.

The O&R and PSEG Long Island lists include oxygen concentrators, ventilators and respirators, dialysis machines, IV feeding and infusion devices and suction machines. Con Edison asks you to register even if electricity is included in the rent, so it can reach you in an outage.

Where can my parent get help paying the bill?

Start with HEAP, then check the Energy Affordability Program (EAP), which knocks money off every monthly bill. A payment plan with the utility is the third piece.

HEAP

HEAP pays part of the heating bill once a season, and it has a separate emergency benefit when a shutoff is coming or fuel is running out. For 2026 to 2027, a one-person household can have gross income up to $3,563 a month, and two people up to $4,659. The base regular benefit goes up $35 for a household with a vulnerable member, which includes anyone 60 or older. The regular benefit opened November 2, 2026, and Emergency HEAP is scheduled to open January 4, 2027. For Emergency HEAP, a household with someone 60 or older must have less than $3,750 in resources. In New York City, call HRA at 718-557-1399. Elsewhere, contact your county Department of Social Services, or the state OTDA HEAP hotline at 1-800-342-3009, weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Our HEAP guide has the full benefit table.

Energy Affordability Program

EAP gives a monthly discount on electric and gas bills from New York's large utilities. DPS says every household that gets HEAP qualifies, as do households on SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, a Veterans Disability or Survivors Pension, Lifeline phone service or federal public housing help. Since January 13, 2026, households below median income can also qualify (area median income for Con Edison and National Grid NYC and Long Island customers). These are the income limits DPS lists as of October 15, 2026:

Household sizeCon Edison and National Grid NYCNational Grid Long IslandNational Grid upstate and all other NY utilities
1$113,400$115,450$69,477
2$129,600$131,950$90,854

DPS says people on certain assistance programs may be enrolled automatically. If you are not sure, call the utility and ask whether the account has the EAP discount. EAP customers are also put on budget billing, which you can leave at any time.

Payment plans

Under HEFPA, a customer whose financial problems kept them from paying can ask for a deferred payment agreement. The utility can refuse one if it believes you can pay, and it can refuse terms of less than $10 a month on the old balance. The down payment generally cannot be more than 15% of what is owed or half the average monthly bill, whichever is greater. The SNAP guide and Medicaid guide can help you line up the benefits that lead to EAP.

Can my mom get a discount on her phone or internet?

Lifeline is a federal program that takes up to $9.25 a month off phone, internet or bundled service. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) says you qualify with household income at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, or if you get SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal public housing assistance or the Veterans and Survivors Pension. One Lifeline benefit is allowed per household, and eligibility is checked every year. Apply through the FCC's National Verifier, linked from the FCC Lifeline page, or call 1-800-234-9473 with application questions. Being on Lifeline also counts toward EAP.

Who do I call if the utility will not help?

Call the utility first. DPS says utilities are required by law to help, and asks you to note the date, the employee's name and what was said. If you cannot settle it, the DPS Office of Consumer Services will take a complaint.

  1. Tell the utility about your parent's age or health. Ask it to code the account for the protections for customers 62 and older, blind or disabled, and register any life-support equipment. Get the confirmation in writing if you can.
  2. Name yourself as a third party. Any customer can name a relative or friend, who agrees in writing, to get copies of shutoff and credit notices. You are not responsible for the bill, but you will see trouble coming. This helps a lot if you live in New Jersey and your parent lives in Rockland or Westchester.
  3. Apply for HEAP and check EAP. Use ACCESS NYC in the city or myBenefits.ny.gov elsewhere, then ask the utility to confirm the EAP discount.
  4. If a shutoff is close, call the PSC hotline. For a final notice saying service will be cut within 48 to 72 hours, call 800-342-3355, weekdays 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Do not use the online form for that.
  5. For other complaints, use the PSC helpline. Call 800-342-3377, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., or file online at dps.ny.gov. Pay the part of the bill that is not in dispute while it is investigated.

While a billing complaint is being looked at, the utility cannot shut off service over the disputed amount, and that protection lasts 15 days after its decision. If you disagree with the DPS decision, you can ask for an informal hearing or review within 15 days, in writing or by phone. For help with home energy costs over the long run, NYS Homes and Community Renewal runs the Weatherization Assistance Program for low-income households (518-474-5700). Ask your county Office for the Aging or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 for help with the forms.

faq.q: Can the utility shut off my mom's heat in the winter in Westchester?
faq.a: It can, but only after strict steps. From November 1 to April 15, the utility must try to reach an adult at home three days before and on the day of a heat shutoff. If harm might result, it must notify Social Services and wait 15 more business days. If everyone in the home is 62 or older, blind or disabled, more protections apply.

faq.q: How do I stop my dad's electric from being shut off in Queens? He's on oxygen.
faq.a: Register his oxygen concentrator with Con Edison right away by calling 1-877-582-6633 or using the life-support form in My Account. A doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or board of health official must certify it within 30 days. If a shutoff is near, call the PSC hotline at 800-342-3355.

faq.q: What is the medical emergency rule for utilities in New York?
faq.a: If a doctor or the local Board of Health tells the utility that losing service would worsen a medical emergency, the utility must keep service on for 30 days. A written certificate must follow within five business days. It can be renewed if the doctor explains the need and you show you cannot pay.

faq.q: Do seniors have to pay a utility deposit in New York?
faq.a: Under HEFPA, a utility cannot require a deposit from a customer 62 or older, unless service was shut off for nonpayment within the past six months. Customers on public assistance or SSI also cannot be required to pay a deposit.

faq.q: What is the Energy Affordability Program?
faq.a: EAP is a monthly discount on electric and gas bills from New York's large utilities. Households on HEAP, SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, a Veterans Disability or Survivors Pension or Lifeline qualify, and since January 2026 so do households below median income. Some people are enrolled automatically, so ask your utility to check.

faq.q: How do I file a complaint against a utility in New York?
faq.a: Call the utility first and write down who you spoke with. If that fails, call the Department of Public Service helpline at 800-342-3377, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., or file online. For a shutoff due within 48 to 72 hours, call the hotline at 800-342-3355.

title: Benefits for older veterans and surviving spouses in New York
seoTitle: NY Veterans Benefits for Seniors and Widows
seoDesc: Free help from NYS Veterans' Services, VA pension with Aid and Attendance, property tax exemptions, veterans homes and burial for older veterans in New York.
dek: Older veterans and their surviving spouses in New York can get a VA pension, extra money for care at home, a property tax break, a bed in a state veterans home and burial in a veterans cemetery. Free advisors will file the paperwork with you.
keyFacts: NYS Veterans' Services advisors: 1-888-838-7697, free
VA Aid and Attendance limit: $29,093 a year for a single veteran (rates effective December 1, 2025)
Alternative veterans exemption: 15% off assessed value, plus 10% for combat service
Four state veterans homes run by DOH, plus a fifth at Stony Brook
Spouses and surviving spouses can be buried in a VA national cemetery
body:
If your mom or dad served in the military, New York and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) offer more help than most families expect. The main benefits for older veterans are a VA pension (with extra money called Aid and Attendance if they need help at home), VA health care, a local property tax exemption, a bed in a state veterans home, and burial in a national or state veterans cemetery. Surviving spouses can qualify for many of the same things.

You do not have to sort this out alone. The New York State Department of Veterans' Services (DVS) has Veterans Benefits Advisors, all veterans themselves, who will prepare and file claims for free. Call 1-888-838-7697 or book a phone or video appointment at veterans.ny.gov.

Who can help us file, and does it cost anything?

Free help comes from two places in New York. DVS runs field offices across the state, and almost every county has its own County Veterans Service Agency. Both will review the veteran's papers, tell you what to apply for, fill out the forms, file the claim and follow up. DVS says its advisors also help appeal an unfavorable decision. DVS also runs a Blind Annuity, a monthly stipend for visually impaired veterans and eligible surviving spouses.

A few county offices close to New Jersey, as listed by DVS:

CountyOfficePhone
Rockland20 Squadron Boulevard, Suite 480, New City845-638-5244
Orange111 Craigville Road, Goshen845-291-2470
Westchester10 County Center Road, Suite 204, White Plains914-813-5145
Putnam110 Old Route 6, Building 3, Room 45, Carmel845-808-1620
ErieRath Office Building, 95 Franklin Street, Suite 800, Buffalo716-858-6363

In the five boroughs, the NYC Department of Veterans' Services runs Veteran Resource Centers, which welcome walk-ins and connect veterans and their families with benefits, services and community resources. Find them at nyc.gov/veterans.

Be careful who you pay

Filing a VA claim should not cost your family anything. DVS and county advisors do it free. Be wary of anyone who charges to "help" with a pension claim or suggests moving your parent's savings to qualify. The VA reviews assets transferred in the three years before a pension claim. A transfer for less than fair value that would have put net worth over the limit can bring a penalty of up to five years with no pension.

What is the VA pension, and who qualifies?

The Veterans Pension is a monthly payment for wartime veterans with limited income and savings. The VA says a veteran can qualify at 65 or older, or at any age with a permanent and total disability, a long-term nursing home stay due to disability, or Social Security Disability or SSI.

The service rules are specific. A veteran who started active duty before September 8, 1980 needs at least 90 days of active duty with at least one day during a wartime period. The VA's wartime periods include World War II (December 7, 1941 to December 31, 1946), Korea (June 27, 1950 to January 31, 1955), Vietnam (November 1, 1955 to May 7, 1975 for service in Vietnam; August 5, 1964 to May 7, 1975 for service elsewhere) and the Gulf War (August 2, 1990 to a date not yet set by law or presidential proclamation).

The VA also looks at net worth. That means savings and property, but not the home, the car or most home furnishings, and it includes a spouse's net worth. For December 1, 2025 to November 30, 2026, the limit is $163,699. It changes each December, so check the current figure on the VA pension rates page.

What about a surviving spouse?

A widow or widower of a wartime veteran can apply for the Survivors Pension. The VA requires that the spouse has not remarried and lived with the veteran from the marriage until the death, though living apart for reasons such as health or work may still be allowed. Income and net worth limits apply here too.

How much extra is Aid and Attendance or Housebound?

Aid and Attendance and Housebound are add-ons to the VA pension. They raise the yearly limit the VA uses to figure the payment. A veteran qualifies for Aid and Attendance if they need another person's help with bathing, eating or dressing, spend much of the day in bed because of illness, live in a nursing home because of lost mental or physical abilities, or have very limited eyesight. Housebound is for a veteran who stays home most of the time because of a permanent disability. You cannot get both.

The VA pays the difference between your income for VA purposes and a limit called the Maximum Annual Pension Rate (MAPR). These are the MAPRs in effect from December 1, 2025. The VA usually raises them each December, so check its rates page for newer figures.

Veteran's situationBasic pensionHouseboundAid and Attendance
No dependents$17,441 a year$21,313 a year$29,093 a year
One dependent (such as a spouse)$22,839 a year$26,710 a year$34,488 a year

Medical costs you pay yourself can lower your counted income. That matters for families paying a home health aide out of pocket. The VA only lets you deduct medical costs above 5% of the MAPR, which it lists as $872 for a veteran with no dependents.

Here is an illustration with the VA's own figures. Say your dad in Yonkers is a widowed Korea veteran with $20,000 a year in Social Security and a pension, and he pays $12,000 a year for an aide. Only the part above $872 counts, so his counted income could fall to about $8,872. Against the $29,093 Aid and Attendance limit, the gap is about $20,221 a year. The VA does the real calculation, so let an advisor run his numbers.

Paying an aide out of pocket can lower your parent's counted income for the VA pension.

To apply, use VA Form 21P-527EZ for the pension and VA Form 21-2680, which a doctor fills out, for Aid and Attendance or Housebound. A veteran in a nursing home also needs VA Form 21-0779. Mail goes to the Department of Veterans Affairs, Pension Intake Center, PO Box 5365, Janesville, WI 53547-5365. If the paperwork will take a while, an intent to file (VA Form 21-0966) can set an earlier start date. For questions, the VA benefits hotline is 800-827-1000, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern.

Can my parent get VA health care, and does it cover dental?

Most veterans who were not dishonorably discharged can enroll. The VA says it has expanded health care to all veterans who meet basic service rules and were exposed to toxins or hazards, including everyone who served in Vietnam, the Gulf War, Iraq or Afghanistan. Veterans who get a VA pension or qualify for Medicaid are placed in a higher priority group.

The VA says having other health insurance does not change the VA health care benefits you can get. It covers routine eye exams and preventive vision tests. It also pays for glasses for some veterans, including those who get the higher pension for Aid and Attendance or Housebound. Dental care is limited to certain groups, such as veterans with a 100% service-connected rating or former prisoners of war. Others enrolled in VA health care can buy reduced-cost dental insurance through the VA Dental Insurance Program.

To enroll, apply online with Form 10-10EZ or call the VA health benefits hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern. See our hearing, vision and dental guide for options outside the VA.

What property tax breaks do New York veterans get?

New York has several veterans property tax exemptions. Each county, city, town, village and school district decides whether to offer them, so ask your assessor. None of them is automatic. You must file with your assessor, and the deadline in most towns is March 1. In New York City, the Department of Finance deadline is March 15.

ExemptionWho it is forWhat it does
Alternative veterans (RP-458-a)Veterans who served in a designated time of war or got an expeditionary medal, their spouses, and un-remarried surviving spouses15% off assessed value, an extra 10% for combat zone service, plus half the VA disability rating, each up to local dollar caps
Cold War veterans (RP-458-b)Veterans who served during the Cold War periodAn exemption on residential property, where the locality offers it
Eligible fundsVeterans and certain other people who bought the property with pension, bonus or insurance moneyA partial exemption
Permanent and total disabilityVeterans the VA rates permanently and totally disabled from serviceA full exemption on the primary residence where offered, for rolls based on taxable status dates on or after October 1, 2026

For the alternative veterans exemption, the home must be the primary residence. The state says it can continue while the owner is away for medical reasons or living in an institution. When the veteran dies, it can continue if the home is in the name of the un-remarried surviving spouse and it stays that spouse's primary residence. You file once. You only re-file if you move or the disability rating changes.

How much does it save in New York City?

The NYC Department of Finance lists the alternative veterans caps for a one to three family home (tax class 1) as $2,880 for the 15% part, $1,920 for the combat part and $9,600 for the disability part. DOF also lists a Cold War veterans exemption for service from September 2, 1945 to December 26, 1991, with the same $2,880 cap on its 15% part. You can apply online from September 28 to March 15. Also look at STAR and Enhanced STAR and the senior citizen homeowners exemption.

What are New York's state veterans homes?

New York's veterans homes are skilled nursing facilities for veterans and their spouses. The state Department of Health says state law also covers veterans' mothers and fathers and un-remarried surviving spouses. The Health Department runs four of the homes. The State University of New York runs a fifth, at Stony Brook.

HomeAddressPhone
Oxford (Chenango County)4211 State Highway 220, Oxford607-843-3100
Batavia (Genesee County)220 Richmond Avenue, Batavia585-345-2000
Montrose (Westchester County)2090 Albany Post Road, Montrose914-788-6000
St. Albans (Queens)17850 Linden Boulevard, Jamaica718-990-0300
Long Island State Veterans Home100 Patriots Road, Stony BrookAdmissions 631-444-8387 (444-VETS)

The Long Island home lists its rules plainly. The applicant must need skilled nursing care. The veteran must have been a New York resident when entering service or for one year before applying, had an honorable discharge and at least 30 days of active service other than training. A spouse or widow married to an eligible veteran for a year before applying can also be admitted, and so can a Gold Star parent. Call each home's admissions office, since rules and waits differ. You can compare any nursing home with our nursing home ratings guide, and read how Medicaid pays for long stays.

Where can a veteran and spouse be buried?

Any veteran who was not dishonorably discharged can be buried in a VA national cemetery, and so can a spouse or surviving spouse, even one who remarried after the veteran died. The VA also provides headstones, markers and medallions. You can apply online now for a pre-need eligibility decision, so the family already has the answer when the time comes.

CemeteryLocationBurial space (VA listing)
Calverton National CemeteryCalverton, Suffolk CountyOpen
Gerald B. H. Solomon Saratoga National CemeterySchuylervilleOpen
Bath National CemeteryBath, Steuben CountyOpen
Western New York National CemeteryCorfu, Genesee CountyOpen
Long Island, St. Albans and Woodlawn (Elmira)Farmingdale, Queens, ElmiraCremation only
NYS Veterans Cemetery, Finger LakesRomulus, Seneca CountyOpen (state run)

The state cemetery in Romulus, run by DVS, takes veterans discharged under other than dishonorable conditions, their legal spouses and eligible dependent children. Service rules apply to veterans who entered after September 7, 1980. DVS says to contact the cemetery for the fee for a dependent's burial, and to call 1-888-838-7697 to talk with an advisor.

The VA also pays burial allowances in some cases, such as when the veteran died while getting a VA pension or compensation. For a death not related to service on or after October 1, 2026, the VA lists a $1,032 burial allowance and $1,032 for a plot. When the death was service connected, the VA lists up to $2,000 for a death on or after September 11, 2001. For a death not related to service, the claim is usually due within two years of the burial. A surviving spouse listed on the veteran's VA profile is paid a set amount automatically once the VA learns of the death.

How do we get started?

  1. Find the discharge papers. Look for the DD-214 or other separation papers. If they are lost, a DVS advisor can help you request them from the National Archives.
  2. Book a free advisor. Call DVS at 1-888-838-7697 or your County Veterans Service Agency. Bring Social Security numbers, marriage and death certificates, and a list of income, savings and medical bills.
  3. File an intent to file. If the paperwork will take time, VA Form 21-0966 sets a possible start date. If the claim is approved, back pay can reach to that date.
  4. Apply for the property tax exemption. File Form RP-458-a with your assessor before March 1 (March 15 with NYC Finance). Attach the DD-214 and any VA disability rating letter.
  5. Plan ahead for care and burial. Call a veterans home's admissions office before a crisis. Apply for VA pre-need burial eligibility so the family has the letter ready.

For general VA questions any time, the MyVA411 line is 800-698-2411, open 24 hours a day. If your parent also needs help at home or with drug costs, see our guides to caregiver support and EPIC.

faq.q: How do I get my dad Aid and Attendance in Westchester?
faq.a: Call the Westchester County Veterans Service Agency at 914-813-5145 or NYS Veterans' Services at 1-888-838-7697 for a free advisor. He must qualify for the VA pension (wartime service, age 65 or disabled, limited income and net worth), and a doctor must complete VA Form 21-2680 showing he needs help with daily activities.

faq.q: My mom is a veteran's widow in Queens. What can she get?
faq.a: She may qualify for the VA Survivors Pension if she did not remarry and meets the income and net worth limits. If the home is in her name and she lives there, she can keep the alternative veterans property tax exemption. She can also be buried with her husband in a national cemetery. NYC Veteran Resource Centers and DVS advisors help free.

faq.q: How much is the VA Aid and Attendance pension?
faq.a: The VA pays the gap between your counted income and a yearly limit. For rates in effect from December 1, 2025, the Aid and Attendance limit is $29,093 for a veteran with no dependents and $34,488 with one dependent. Unreimbursed medical costs above 5% of the limit lower counted income. The rates usually change each December.

faq.q: Is the veterans property tax exemption automatic in New York?
faq.a: No. You must file Form RP-458-a with your assessor, usually by March 1, or apply with the NYC Department of Finance by March 15. You only file once unless you move or the disability rating changes. Each town, county and school district decides whether to offer it.

faq.q: Who can live in a New York State veterans home?
faq.a: The homes take veterans and their spouses who need skilled nursing care, and in some cases veterans' parents and un-remarried surviving spouses. The Long Island home requires New York residency at entry into service or for a year before applying, an honorable discharge and at least 30 days of active service.

faq.q: Can my mom be buried with my dad in a national cemetery in New York?
faq.a: Yes. The VA says a spouse or surviving spouse of an eligible veteran can be buried in a VA national cemetery, even if she remarried after he died. Calverton, Saratoga, Bath and Western New York have open space; Long Island, St. Albans and Woodlawn take cremated remains only.
